_Why can a machine that completes every trial still lack the evidence to be allowed among people?_

A successful trial shows what a machine did under the conditions it happened to meet, while permission to operate is a claim about every condition it may meet next. Thousands of clean runs on a dry floor say nothing about the stop on a floor no trial touched, and a brake that stopped the machine last month may not stop it inside the same distance after its lining wears. A machine granted authority on demonstrations therefore carries untested premises into service, where the first test of each one is the event it was meant to prevent. Deciding to deploy requires stating which physical claims the evidence supports, under which conditions and for how long, refusing or narrowing operation wherever a premise remains unknown, and withdrawing the grant when brakes wear, sensors shift, or software changes. At the causal boundary, authority must expire when its physical justification does, because a later software correction cannot undo motion already produced.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Construct a claim-argument-evidence (CAE) safety case as an auditable engineering assertion DAG linking bounded operating envelopes to qualified measurements, analysis, and operating conditions
- Distinguish input provenance from premise status, and select the verdict (`UNCOND`, `COND`, or `REFUSE`) the supported operating claim permits
- Join task-success, cycle-time, and intervention evidence to the physical measurements and restrictions supporting a conditional release
- Specify standing-condition cadences and validated responses, from brake wear to calibration drift, separately from execution leases
- Diagnose unsupported warrants, hidden contextual assumptions, and compound defeaters through adversarial review of a release argument
- Specify the records a release manifest binds by digest and the conditions under which its gate refuses motion
- Determine which claims a policy or software update reopens, and why shadow operation cannot substitute for closed-loop qualification

:::

## The Decision to Deploy {#sec-release-decision-to-deploy}

Verification left the machine with a signed set of fault records. Each pairs an observed trace under an injected fault (a stalled proposer, a stale frame, lost fieldbus frames, a sagging bus) with an oracle fixed before the trial, and the set names the operating regimes no trial reached. Beside it sit the records the earlier chapters produced: the authority record of arbitration and fallback outcomes, the placement record of compute scheduling and isolation, and the evaluation record of closed-loop task performance. Those records say how the machine behaved under the conditions tested. They do not say which operating claim the machine may now be granted, because a fault record proves nothing outside the envelope it sampled, and an untested mode is a gap rather than a pass. Offline validation accuracy and clean laboratory demonstrations sit in the same position. Release is the step that decides, claim by claim, what this evidence licenses across a named operational design domain.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The empirical verification evidence backing release claims is established in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

That step is a threshold every machine operating among humans eventually crosses, the point where builders formally grant it authority to act outside the laboratory. In conventional software engineering, deployment is largely reversible; an operator can recall a defective build within minutes, bounding the cost of failure to the time required to roll back the binary. For physical systems, that release grant differs. Every action authorized by the runtime delivers energy across the causal boundary into the physical environment. When a release decision errs, the failure appears as an actuator driving past an obstacle clearance line or a gripper exerting uncalibrated force against human tissue, and no software rollback can recall kinetic energy already transferred. Aerospace, rail transit, and industrial robotics manage this risk through an explicit safety case, a structured and auditable argument stating what the machine is claimed to do, under what operating conditions, and on what evidence. Physical AI inherits this burden with an added difficulty. A learned policy cannot be proven safe by inspecting its weights, and finite field trials cannot surface every rare tail failure, which is where the worst consequences lie.

The warehouse mobile manipulator shows why past operational success cannot by itself license deployment. In an active logistics depot it must travel narrow aisles past protruding rack ends, unlatch a spring-latched cage door, and hand a ceramic mug to a human coworker. Each subtask turns on a distinct physical claim: a stopping distance inside the clear distance at maximum payload, a bounded peak force on the latch, and a limited contact force during the handover. A spotless test run shows only that the machine executed those motions under the exact conditions of that single trial. A sound release decision must instead bound the physical variations the machine will face in production and show that verified plant dynamics and low-level safety interlocks keep risk within limits across that entire envelope.

A deployed system must also do useful work inside its certified envelope. Closed-loop evaluation logs show whether an end-to-end policy completes its tasks, how often humans must intervene, and which environmental conditions cause the policy to break down. Engineers must weigh these task metrics against the speed limits, payload caps, and spatial restrictions required by the safety case. A mobile base that trips safety stops every few meters avoids collisions while failing its service target; conversely, an agile policy that finishes every nominal trial cannot be given actuator authority until deterministic guardrails enforce safe bounds during perception failures. The release decision brings these two requirements together into one operating profile.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The closed-loop evaluation record of task success, intervention rates, and breakdown conditions is established in @sec-evaluation-logs.
:::

Because different facilities have different lighting, floor friction, and foot traffic, an initial release case applies to a single facility, drawing on its site clearance surveys, loaded braking trials, calibrated impact-force measurements, and cryptographically signed fault records. Rather than boiling deployment readiness down to a single benchmark score, the release decision is a bounded, revocable judgment that determines which operational claims the available evidence actually supports, under what physical conditions, and for how long. This chapter builds that decision in the order an adjudicator meets it: the claims are first written as testable physical inequalities over a bounded operating envelope, then organized into an argument whose every link names its evidence. The argument resolves into one of three verdicts (full operational authorization, restricted operation inside enforced limits, or refusal), and standing conditions define when a granted verdict expires. A worked adjudication applies all of this to the running machine, an adversarial review tries to break whatever case survives, and a signed release manifest binds the final decision to the executing machine so that every later software update, retrained checkpoint, or hardware modification passes through the same gate.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The signed fault records a release case consumes are established in @sec-verification-fault-manifest.
:::

## Physical Criteria for Release {#sec-release-question}

A deployment review that signs off on aggregate benchmark scores or smooth demo videos leaves the machine with no testable rule for when it may move. At a rack end, the base must stop inside the available clearance; during handover, the arm must stay within the assessed contact-force limit; and both claims depend on the permission path finishing its check before its deadline. Together, those requirements give release authorization three testable physical criteria:
$$\StoppingDistance(\SpeedAtDetection, \PrebrakeDelay, \CredibleBrakingDeceleration, \LocalizationBound, \TrackingErrorBound) \le \ClearDistance, \quad \CollaborativeContactForce(\SpeedAtDetection, \EffectiveImpactMass, \HertzianContactStiffness) \le \AssessedContactForceLimit, \quad \WorstCasePermissionCycleTime \le \CompletionDeadline.$$ {#eq-release-authorization-criterion}

The first term abbreviates the full stopping budget of @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope, whose protective margin is charged as well. In the third criterion, $\WorstCasePermissionCycleTime$ is the worst-case execution time of one permission-path cycle and $\CompletionDeadline$ the deadline that cycle must meet inside its tick (@sec-enforcement-loop-budget). A permission computed after its deadline cannot be credited for that cycle, and the qualified fallback must contain the resulting delay.

Because each criterion is a physical inequality, release authorization cannot rest on intuition, demonstrations, or aggregate benchmark scores. Authorizing deployment requires an auditable safety argument that links every inequality to measured observation ages, worst-case execution time bounds, empirical braking and contact trials, and a validated fallback. These physical bounds also depend on the individual machine's calibration: its camera and lidar sensor transforms, joint encoder zero offsets, and motor torque constants. A lost or drifted calibration invalidates the certified stopping budget even when software binaries remain unchanged. A sensor mount that shifts in service erodes the localization allowance $\LocalizationBound$ (@sec-release-calibration-drift), and a firmware update that overwrites measured sensor extrinsics and joint offsets\index{Over-the-air update!calibration retention} invalidates the budget just as quickly. The deployment pipeline must therefore preserve and re-verify calibration records before restoring the operating permit (@sec-release-modular-safety-cases).

For the warehouse mobile manipulator, the release question asks whether empirical and analytical evidence satisfies these criteria for each of its three tasks inside a scoped operating envelope. The release case defines the assessed physical bounds, the specified hardware fault model, and the validated permission and fallback ladder. This argument is the safety case, which @sec-release-assurance-grammar gives a formal structure, and it justifies granting a revocable operating permit while those physical conditions hold. The permit is the signed authority under which the permission path may admit the policy's tracking commands (@sec-release-three-verdicts). Finite test runs cannot establish protection against uncharacterized or unmodeled hazards.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-contact-premises
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONTACT PREMISES INHERITED FROM THE ENFORCEMENT RECORD
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: every contact number this chapter quotes (@sec-release-question,
# │          @tbl-16-cae-scorecard, @sec-release-case-worked-full). The
# │          derivation is taught in @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact.
# │ Goal:    read the contact premises exactly as the enforcement chapter
# │          derives them, so release adjudicates and never re-derives.
# │ Show:    nothing directly; the release cells below read this class.
# │ How:     mirrors calc-enforcement-contact-force (EnforcementContactForce)
# │          line for line: same MLSysIM functions, same registry inputs, same
# │          guards. Chapters render in separate kernels, so the class is
# │          rebuilt here; the identical guards make any drift between the
# │          two chapters fail the build. Edit both cells together.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile,
    calc_reduced_mass,
    calc_transient_impact_force,
    calc_transient_contact_speed_limit,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementContactForce:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_latch = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: chosen (guarded approach)
    v_latch_high = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (policy's proposed approach)
    k_latch = AISLE.k_latch  # category: illustrative
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative
    t_contact = AISLE.t_contact_response  # category: illustrative (contact loop)
    f_lim = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative
    m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass  # category: derived
    m_hand = AISLE.m_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    k_hand = AISLE.k_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    f_contact = AISLE.f_contact_criterion  # category: chosen
    v_handover = AISLE.v_handover  # category: chosen (handover approach under accept_item)
    tcp_limit = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen (free-space TCP limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    stop_lo = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(v_latch, scenario=AISLE)
    stop_hi = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(v_latch_high, scenario=AISLE)
    df_dt = stop_lo["df_dt"]
    f_cmd = stop_lo["f_at_brake_onset"]
    x_rem = stop_lo["x_remaining"]
    a_arm = stop_lo["a_arm_needed"]
    t_arm_stop = stop_lo["t_arm_stop"]
    f_cmd_hi = stop_hi["f_at_brake_onset"]
    a_arm_hi = stop_hi["a_arm_needed"]
    m_red = calc_reduced_mass(m_eff, m_hand).to(kilogram)
    f_at_tcp_limit = calc_transient_impact_force(tcp_limit, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(newton)
    f_ratio = (f_at_tcp_limit / f_contact).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    f_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(v_handover, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(newton)
    f_handover_clamped = calc_transient_impact_force(v_handover, m_eff, k_hand).to(newton)
    v_ceiling = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_contact, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(meter / second)
    v_ceiling_clamped = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_contact, m_eff, k_hand).to(meter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (identical to calc-enforcement-contact-force) ─────────────
    check(abs(f_cmd.to(newton).magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake onset, guarded approach, is 39 N.")
    check(abs(x_rem.to(millimeter).magnitude - 0.1525) < 5e-5, "Remaining latch compression is 0.15 mm.")
    check(abs(a_arm.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 2.95) < 5e-3, "The guarded stop needs about 3 m/s^2 (2.95).")
    check(abs(t_arm_stop.to(millisecond).magnitude - 10.0) < 0.5, "The guarded stop takes about 10 ms.")
    check(abs(f_cmd_hi.to(newton).magnitude - 95.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake onset, unsupported approach, is 95 N.")
    check(abs(a_arm_hi.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-6, "The unsupported approach needs 400 m/s^2.")
    check(f_cmd < f_lim and f_cmd_hi < f_lim, "Both approaches reach brake onset below the latch limit.")
    check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Arm effective contact mass is 12.0 kg.")
    check(abs(m_red.magnitude - 0.5714) < 5e-5, "Hand-arm reduced mass is 0.571 kg.")
    check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 207.02) < 0.01, "Transient force at the TCP limit is 207 N.")
    check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "Transient handover force is 20.7 N.")
    check(abs(f_handover_clamped.magnitude - 94.87) < 0.01, "Clamped handover force is 94.9 N.")
    check(f_handover < f_contact < f_handover_clamped, "Transient passes and clamped fails the criterion.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Free-hand ceiling is 0.24 m/s.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped-hand ceiling is 0.053 m/s.")
    check(v_ceiling_clamped < v_handover < v_ceiling, "The handover cap sits between the clamped and free-hand ceilings.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Raw quantities only; each release cell formats what it quotes.
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-operating-envelope
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S OPERATING ENVELOPE FOR RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question (envelope and conditional-zone paragraphs),
# │          @tbl-16-odd-invariants, the contact-criteria paragraph after it, and
# │          the binding-contract paragraphs of @sec-release-three-verdicts, and
# │          the empirical-sufficiency probe of @sec-release-adversarial-review.
# │ Goal: Scope the release case to the running machine's operating envelope.
# │ Show: aisle speed and its ceiling, tote-rack payload, the friction bands and
# │       the inspected-floor ceiling, the clear distance, the latch and handover
# │       speeds with their limits, the slow-downs before a takeover, and the
# │       restricted speed on inspected floors.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; ceilings from the finished stopping budgets
# │      (Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed and ...InspectedFloor: the
# │      jerk-limited S-curve stop, jerk bound = the reference C2 polynomial's
# │      peak jerk at the drive limit, and the three overheads); mu_min =
# │      a_brake/g (calc_required_friction).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_velocity, fmt_length, fmt_mass, fmt_force, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, check
from mlsysim.physics.drivetrain import calc_required_friction

class ReleaseEnvelope:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
    AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
    g_std = (1 * standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)
    STOP = Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed  # category: illustrative (finished budget at the aisle speed)
    INSPECTED = Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopInspectedFloor  # category: illustrative (same budget, inspected-floor traction)
    v_restricted = (
        Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopRestricted.speed
    )  # category: chosen (restricted mode on inspected floors, the value @sec-frontier uses)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE: ceilings and friction bands ───────────────────────────────────
    # Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
    j_brake = STOP.jerk.to(meter / second**3)
    overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
    v_ceiling = STOP.result.speed_ceiling.to(meter / second)
    mu_min = calc_required_friction(AISLE.a_brake)
    # Optimistic all-weight-on-driven-wheels traction screen; actual loaded stopping needs qualification.
    # The jerk bound belongs to the load and is unchanged.
    a_inspected = INSPECTED.deceleration.to(meter / second**2)
    v_inspected_ceiling = INSPECTED.result.speed_ceiling.to(meter / second)
    # Handover ceilings are enforcement premises (calc-release-contact-premises).
    v_handover_ceiling = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling
    v_handover_ceiling_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling_clamped

    # ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose and the table ──────────────────
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, "Unconditional aisle speed ceiling is 1.44 m/s")
    check(AISLE.v_aisle < v_ceiling, "Chosen aisle speed sits under its ceiling")
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction floor is 0.204")
    check(mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Dry concrete exceeds the friction floor")
    check(mu_min > AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, "Inspected floor requires speed restriction")
    check(abs(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, "Restricted ceiling on inspected floors is 1.23 m/s")
    check(abs(a_inspected.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 1.1768) < 5e-5, "Inspected-floor deceleration mu*g is 1.18 m/s^2")
    check(a_inspected < AISLE.a_brake, "The inspected floor, not the brake, caps the deceleration")
    check(v_restricted < v_inspected_ceiling, "Chosen restricted mode sits under its ceiling")
    check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Transient (free-hand) handover ceiling is 0.24 m/s")
    check(AISLE.v_handover < v_handover_ceiling, "Chosen handover speed sits under its transient ceiling")
    check(abs(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped-hand handover ceiling is 0.053 m/s")
    check(AISLE.v_handover > v_handover_ceiling_clamped, "Chosen handover speed exceeds the clamped ceiling, so clamping must be excluded")
    check(abs(RM.loaded_mass.to(kilogram).magnitude - 368.0) < 1e-9, "Running-machine loaded mass is 368 kg")
    check(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop < AISLE.v_aisle, "Slow-down before an in-loop takeover")
    check(AISLE.mu_oil_film < AISLE.mu_inspected_floor < mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Friction bands are ordered")
    check(abs(AISLE.v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "Signed aisle speed 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(AISLE.d_clear.to(meter).magnitude - 1.10) < 1e-9, "Clear distance 1.10 m")
    check(
        abs(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.75) < 1e-9,
        "In-loop takeover slow-down 0.75 m/s (Delta_da-charged ceiling, rounded down)",
    )
    check(abs(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.15) < 1e-9, "Out-of-loop takeover slow-down 0.15 m/s")
    check(abs(AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Permission tick 1 ms")
    check(AISLE.t_tick < AISLE.t_lease, "Servo tick sits inside the chunk lease")
    check(abs(RM.onboard_payload_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity is 50 kg")
    check(
        abs(AISLE.mu_dry - 0.60) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor - 0.12) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_oil_film - 0.05) < 1e-9,
        "Friction bands 0.60, 0.12, 0.05",
    )
    check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_approach.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded latch approach 0.03 m/s")
    check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_high.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Unsupported latch approach 0.10 m/s")
    check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Latch tripwire 15 N")
    check(abs(AISLE.t_contact_response.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Contact-loop response 2 ms")
    check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit 100 N")
    check(abs(AISLE.v_handover.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Handover speed 0.10 m/s")
    check(abs(AISLE.f_contact_criterion.to(newton).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Handover criterion 50 N")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_takeover_out_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(RM.onboard_payload_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_inspected_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, precision=2)
    mu_oil_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_oil_film, precision=2)
    v_inspected_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    a_inspected_str = fmt_acceleration(a_inspected, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    g_str = fmt_acceleration(g_std, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_high, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_clamped_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)

# Module-level exports for downstream cells
v_restricted = ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted
overhead_loc = ReleaseEnvelope.overhead_loc
v_handover_ceiling_clamped = ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_clamped
mu_min = ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min
g_std = ReleaseEnvelope.g_std
j_brake = ReleaseEnvelope.j_brake
a_inspected = ReleaseEnvelope.a_inspected
v_ceiling = ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling
v_handover_ceiling = ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling
v_inspected_ceiling = ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling
```

A release case is scoped by the operating envelope: the target operational design domain (ODD)\index{Operational design domain!release envelope} paired with the machine's internal hardware, thermal, and timing invariants. Deployment release authorizes a system configuration under standing operating conditions, complementing rather than replacing the short execution leases that bound individual action chunks. Site inspections, calibration checks, and per-tick permission checks operate at the distinct cadences dictated by their respective failure mechanisms. The envelope also fixes what each of the three possible verdicts, defined in @sec-release-three-verdicts, refers to. Unconditional operation (`UNCOND`) covers the full verified envelope. Conditional operation (`COND`) covers a separately evidenced subset with constrained kinematics or environmental fences. Refusal (`REFUSE`) covers none of it.\index{Operational design domain!release verdicts} For the mobile manipulator, the proposed nominal operating envelope specifies aisle travel up to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (chosen; see the Reader Guide) with the tote rack loaded to at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`. It also specifies floors surveyed to a friction coefficient of at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str` and travel past rack ends with at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` of clear distance. The friction floor is an optimistic screen obtained by dividing the required braking deceleration by standard gravity under the assumption that all vehicle weight rests on the driven wheels. Because passive casters carry a share of the normal load without contributing braking force, the driven wheels must generate the total stopping force from a smaller normal load, so actual qualification must include loaded wheel forces, drive settings, and stopping traces. For manipulation, the proposed envelope specifies door approaches at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str` and coworker handovers at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` tool center point (TCP) speed.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The operational design domain and its known absences are established in @sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability-geometry.
:::

Inside these boundaries, the learned neural policy proposes actions across the nominal task envelope, but every proposed action requires independent, per-tick permission from an isolated safety enforcer. Mode-specific conditions (@tbl-16-odd-invariants) narrow that envelope. The takeover analysis of @sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines supplies candidate intervention speeds, screening an in-loop request at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` and an out-of-loop crawl at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_out_str`. Neither screen qualifies as a standalone release limit, because each depends on a human response time that the release case has not measured. The in-loop slow-down holds only for an operator answering an expected stimulus, and the out-of-loop crawl already fails the 99th-percentile response. The robust design therefore runs the base's own local stop first and hands over control from standstill, where waiting costs time but no clearance. The restricted mode of a `COND` verdict narrows the envelope further. On a floor characterized only through the site inspection regime, the machine runs at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` optimistic all-weight inspected-floor screen, while still charging dispatch-to-admission delay and maintaining a positive stopping reserve.

The rules in @tbl-16-odd-invariants follow a strict priority ladder: refusal conditions override mode-specific restrictions, which in turn override nominal limits. Because speed ranges overlap across operational contexts, these thresholds define operating modes rather than disjoint numerical intervals. The payload row shows how a mode differs from an interval. If the tote-rack load estimate has gone stale since the last pick, the base may not transit, because its stopping budget assumes a known mass. The stationary arm may keep working under its own separately evidenced claim. An invalid estimate or a measured overload refuses both. A conditional state restricts admitted proposals through enforcer clamping. A refusal state revokes the operating permit, so the permission path admits no further tracking commands, and commands a validated fallback trajectory. Onboard wheel slip estimation cannot provide prospective clearance guarantees because it detects low friction only *after* traction has already been lost. A thin film of clear oil ($\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) can be visually indistinguishable from dry concrete to the navigation cameras. By the time a loaded base moving at aisle speed (`{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str`) initiates braking on an oil patch and measures slip, it has already committed to a stopping distance that exceeds the clear distance. Consequently, the release case must justify how site surveys, contamination exclusion, and bounded inspection and response procedures preserve the assessed friction floor throughout the authorized interval. Periodic surveys alone cannot exclude a spill between inspections.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The ladder of resident fallback responses that a refusal commands is established in @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder.
:::

The safety case must also document machine behavior when operation encounters an envelope boundary. Event-triggered edge telemetry\index{Edge telemetry!event-triggered buffer}\index{Black-box recorder!pre- and post-trigger capture} freezes circular buffer traces for post-incident review (@sec-release-data-curation-flywheel), while the deterministic permission path enforces physical boundaries in real time. @Tbl-16-odd-invariants summarizes the physical dimensions maintained by runtime monitors and administrative site controls. Internal environmental conditions, such as ambient temperature, DC bus rail voltage, and compute system-on-chip (SoC) utilization, enter the release case through fault injection and stress tests conducted across their qualified ranges.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The internal qualification ranges for temperature, bus voltage, and compute load that the release case inherits are established in @sec-verification-operating-envelope.
:::

\Needspace{28\baselineskip}

| Envelope Dimension / Invariant | Nominal Envelope                                                                                                                          | Conditional Boundary                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Hard Refusal                                                                                                                                                                                           | Runtime Monitor & Rate                                                                 | Enforcer Action & Latency                                                      |
|:-------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Aisle Speed**                | $\SpeedAtDetection\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str`                                                                             | Preliminary takeover screens: `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` in-loop and `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_out_str` out-of-loop; the robust design stops before any handover                                                                | Measured speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling_str`), or invalid speed estimate                                                   | Encoders and IMU, every `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_tick_str` permission tick          | Clamp admitted speed; refuse above the signed speed                            |
| **Floor Friction**             | Surveyed $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str` (dry concrete near `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_dry_str`) | Qualified assessment and maintained site regime ($\CoulombFrictionCoefficient\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`): restricted `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` ceiling | Unsurveyed floor or reported film; a clear oil film ($\CoulombFrictionCoefficient\approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) can evade the installed cameras                                       | Floor survey and site spill procedure; no on-board measurement                         | Restrict speed by floor zone; refuse the aisle                                 |
| **Tote-Rack Payload**          | $0\le \Mass\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, valid load estimate (total at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.m1_str`)             | Estimate stale since the last pick: stationary arm tasks only                                                                                                                                                                                                | Load above capacity or invalid estimate                                                                                                                                                                | Rack load cells, at each pick                                                          | Refuse aisle transit until re-weighed                                          |
| **Rack-End Clearance**         | Surveyed $\ClearDistance\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` at every rack end                                                     | Shorter surveyed clearance: lower signed speed from the same budget                                                                                                                                                                                          | Unsurveyed rack end, or obstacle inside the clear distance                                                                                                                                             | Site survey; lidar and navigation camera at frame rate                                 | Speed limit per rack end; stop for a detected obstacle                         |
| **Door Latch Approach**        | $\SpeedAtDetection\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str`, strike plate at its nominal position                                       | Original policy: nominal plate only; changed recovery candidate needs its own evaluation and release case                                                                                                                                                    | `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_high_str` approach or plate condition outside the selected policy case                                                                                               | Arm contact-force sensing in the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_contact_str` contact loop | Trip at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_trip_str`; refuse the unsupported approach |
| **Coworker Handover**          | TCP speed $\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` under `accept_item`                                                             | Coworker present without `accept_item`: hold short of the handover point                                                                                                                                                                                     | TCP speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` (transient ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`), or a clamping geometry outside the assessed transient case | Joint encoders every permission tick; arm contact-force sensing                        | Clamp TCP speed; refuse above the signed speed                                 |

: **Operating envelope of the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Refusal rules take priority over restricted-mode rules and nominal limits. Conditional operation requires every relied-on premise to remain supported; stale payload evidence permits only separately supported stationary work, while an invalid estimate or overload refuses. The takeover speeds are preliminary screens, not qualified motion limits. The friction floor and inspected-floor ceiling assume all weight on driven wheels and require loaded stopping qualification. The displayed speed ceilings are partial calculations before dispatch-to-admission delay; signed limits require that delay and a positive reserve. Sensor rates and stopping response are plant validation obligations. {#tbl-16-odd-invariants tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

The nominal latch row in @tbl-16-odd-invariants scopes the baseline policy release case. Although the separately stipulated recovery campaign in @sec-evaluation-recovery-update evaluates a changed candidate across nominal and displaced-plate conditions, that experimental provenance does not silently extend the contact-force or timing bounds established here. Deploying the recovery policy requires its own evaluation and safety case update.

A defensible release claim must specify its plant dynamics, assumed contact geometry, and modeled fault set. The release case for the mobile manipulator rests on three criteria. The base stops inside the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance before reaching a pedestrian who has stepped out at a rack end and stopped. The arm unlatches the door without exceeding the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_latch_limit_str` structural limit. An item handover does not exceed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_contact_str` of peak contact force against the coworker. The base's stopping claim assumes that the person, once in the path, stands still. A person who keeps walking toward the moving base closes the gap during the whole reaction and braking interval. As @sec-enforcement-composite-budget showed, sizing the budget for that approach would cut the aisle speed to the much lower walking-person ceiling. The site therefore controls aisle-end crossings procedurally, and that site crossing rule is itself a premise the release case must evidence. A complete release argument demonstrates which human contacts are excluded before impact, which detected contacts fall within the compliance model, and which single-point faults trigger the isolated fallback. Halting motion after impact occurs does not reduce the initial shock force.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-biomechanical-impact-envelope
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HANDOVER CONTACT FORCE AND THE BASE'S STOPPING SPARE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question (the handover-premise paragraph and the
# │          spare-spent-as-delay paragraph), and the refusal paragraph of
# │          @sec-release-three-verdicts (the deceleration the budget assumes).
# │          The contact-force derivation itself lives in
# │          calc-enforcement-contact-force (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact);
# │          this cell reads it through calc-release-contact-premises.
# │ Goal: Restate the handover premises release inherits, and show how little
# │       input error the base's finished budget can absorb at aisle speed.
# │ Show: unbraked force at the free-space TCP limit and at the handover speed;
# │       budget and spare at 1.3 m/s; the delay and the deceleration shortfall
# │       that each consume the spare.
# │ How: contact forces read from EnforcementContactForce (free hand: reduced
# │      mass of hand and arm; clamped: the arm's effective mass alone); the
# │      finished budget Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed (the
# │      jerk-limited S-curve stop, jerk bound = the reference C2 polynomial's
# │      peak jerk at the drive limit, and the three overheads) and its
# │      ...WithDispatch variant; the break-even deceleration (min_deceleration)
# │      solves v^2/(2a) + v a/(2j) = braking room with j fixed.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_stiffness,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_multiple,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_sci_qty,
    fmt_jerk,
    check,
)
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_scurve_stop_distance

class BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
    AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
    STOP = Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed  # category: illustrative (finished budget at the aisle speed)
    DISPATCH = Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopWithDispatch  # category: illustrative (same budget, Delta_da charged)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE: contact forces, then the budget at aisle speed ────────────────
    # Contact premises from the enforcement record (calc-release-contact-premises).
    m_eff = EnforcementContactForce.m_eff
    f_at_tcp_limit = EnforcementContactForce.f_at_tcp_limit
    f_ratio = EnforcementContactForce.f_ratio
    f_at_handover = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover
    f_at_handover_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover_clamped
    v_handover_ceiling = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling
    v_handover_ceiling_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling_clamped

    # Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
    stop = STOP.result
    j_brake = stop.jerk.to(meter / second**3)
    c2_braking = stop.scurve_travel.to(meter)
    overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
    d_reaction = stop.delay_travel.to(millimeter)
    budget_aisle = stop.required_distance.to(millimeter)
    spare_aisle = stop.spare.to(millimeter)
    t_spare = stop.delay_spare.to(millisecond)
    spare_share = (spare_aisle / AISLE.d_clear).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    # Deceleration at which the budget exactly fills the clear distance, jerk bound
    # fixed: the smaller root of (v/(2j)) a^2 - room a + v^2/2 = 0, on the branch
    # where distance falls as a rises (a < sqrt(v j)).
    braking_room = stop.braking_room.to(meter)
    a_break_even = stop.min_deceleration.to(meter / second**2)
    a_shortfall = stop.deceleration_shortfall
    # Notebook terms (nbk-release-aisle-spare): the two S-curve pieces, the delay
    # split, and the dispatch-to-admission allocation Delta_da charged against the
    # partial spare (the same allocation @sec-enforcement charges).
    d_brake_quad = stop.braking_travel.to(millimeter)
    d_brake_jerk = stop.jerk_ramp_travel.to(millimeter)
    t_renewal_to_onset = Scenarios.WarehouseRenewalReferencedStop.delay.to(millisecond)
    delta_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (allocation of @sec-placement-dispatch-admission)
    travel_da = stop.travel_over(delta_da).to(millimeter)
    reserve_aisle = DISPATCH.result.spare.to(millimeter)
    t_reserve = DISPATCH.result.delay_spare.to(millisecond)
    d_braking = c2_braking.to(millimeter)
    d_loc = AISLE.delta_loc.to(millimeter)
    d_track = AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter)
    d_margin = AISLE.delta_margin.to(millimeter)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear.to(millimeter)
    budget = budget_aisle
    spare = spare_aisle

    # ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose ────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Effective contact mass is 12.0 kg")
    check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 207.02) < 0.01, "Transient force at the TCP limit")
    check(abs(f_ratio - 4.14) < 0.01, "About 4.1x the 50 N criterion")
    check(abs(f_at_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "Transient handover force is 20.7 N")
    check(abs(f_at_handover_clamped.magnitude - 94.87) < 0.01, "Clamped handover force is 94.9 N")
    check(f_at_handover < AISLE.f_contact_criterion < f_at_handover_clamped, "Transient passes, clamped fails the criterion")
    check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Transient handover ceiling is 0.24 m/s")
    check(abs(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped handover ceiling is 0.053 m/s")
    check(abs(j_brake.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, "Jerk bound is the reference polynomial's 7.11 m/s^3 peak")
    check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 968.9925) < 5e-3, "Finished budget at 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(spare_aisle.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(t_spare.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, "Spare spent as delay is 100.8 ms")
    # margin_aisle_budget_spare_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types the five terms and the spare
    check(abs(d_reaction.magnitude - 173.68) < 5e-3, "Reaction travel 173.7 mm at 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(c2_braking.to(millimeter).magnitude - 605.3125) < 5e-3, "S-curve braking 605.3 mm")
    check(abs(AISLE.delta_loc.to(millimeter).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Localization allowance 50 mm")
    check(abs(AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Tracking allowance 40 mm")
    check(abs(AISLE.delta_margin.to(millimeter).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Physical margin 100 mm")
    check(0.11 < spare_share < 0.125, "The spare is about an eighth of the clear distance")
    check(AISLE.v_aisle >= a_break_even**2 / j_brake, "Break-even stop stays in the trapezoidal regime")
    check(
        abs((calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, a_break_even, j_brake) - braking_room).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6,
        "At the break-even deceleration the S-curve stop fills the braking room exactly",
    )
    check(abs(a_break_even.magnitude - 1.386) < 5e-4, "Break-even deceleration is 1.386 m/s^2")
    check(abs(a_shortfall - 0.307) < 5e-4, "A 31 percent deceleration shortfall fills the spare")
    check(AISLE.v_aisle >= AISLE.a_brake**2 / j_brake, "Aisle stop is in the trapezoidal regime, so the two-term S-curve form applies")
    check(abs((d_brake_quad + d_brake_jerk - c2_braking).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6, "The two S-curve pieces sum to the braking term")
    check(abs(d_brake_quad.magnitude - 422.5) < 5e-3 and abs(d_brake_jerk.magnitude - 182.8125) < 5e-3, "S-curve pieces 422.5 and 182.8 mm")
    check(abs(AISLE.tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 1e-9, "Pre-brake delay 133.6 ms")
    check(abs((AISLE.perception_age + t_renewal_to_onset - AISLE.tau_delay).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Delay = age + renewal-to-onset")
    check(abs(braking_room.to(millimeter).magnitude - 736.32) < 5e-3, "Braking room 736.3 mm")
    check(abs(travel_da.magnitude - 82.304) < 5e-3, "Delta_da travel 82.3 mm at 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(reserve_aisle.magnitude - 48.7036) < 5e-3, "Reserve 48.7 mm after Delta_da")
    check(abs(t_reserve.magnitude - 37.464) < 5e-3, "Reserve 37.5 ms at aisle speed")
    check(0 < reserve_aisle < spare_aisle, "Delta_da leaves a positive but smaller reserve")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    f_tcp_str = fmt_force(round(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude) * newton, precision=0)
    f_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(f_ratio, precision=1)
    f_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_at_handover, precision=1)
    f_handover_clamped_str = fmt_force(f_at_handover_clamped, precision=1)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_clamped_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_str = fmt_latency(round(t_spare.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_break_even_str = fmt_acceleration(a_break_even, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    a_shortfall_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(a_shortfall, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    # Notebook strings (nbk-release-aisle-spare)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.perception_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    j_brake_str = fmt_jerk(j_brake, unit=meter / second**3, precision=2)
    d_reaction_str = fmt_length(d_reaction, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_brake_quad_str = fmt_length(d_brake_quad, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_brake_jerk_str = fmt_length(d_brake_jerk, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_braking_str = fmt_length(c2_braking, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_loc_str = fmt_length(AISLE.delta_loc, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_track_str = fmt_length(AISLE.eps_track, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_margin_str = fmt_length(AISLE.delta_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_clear_mm_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    braking_room_str = fmt_length(braking_room, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    delta_da_str = fmt_latency(delta_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    travel_da_str = fmt_length(travel_da, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    reserve_str = fmt_length(reserve_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_reserve_str = fmt_latency(t_reserve, unit=millisecond, precision=1)

# Module-level exports for downstream cells
budget_aisle = BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.budget_aisle
spare_aisle = BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_aisle
t_renewal_to_onset = BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_renewal_to_onset
j_brake = BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.j_brake
m_eff = BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.m_eff
overhead_loc = BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.overhead_loc
v_handover_ceiling = BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling
```

The contact criteria arrive as premises from the enforcement record rather than as calculations derived during release review. The spring-mass impact peak that grows linearly with approach speed (@eq-training-impact-peak) was first met as the soft-spring exploit of the latch simulator. @Sec-enforcement-intentional-contact specializes it to an unbraked elastic contact with a coworker's hand (@eq-release-unbraked-force), using the arm's effective mass and the ISO/TS 15066 biomechanical hand model.[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech] The release case evaluates the operational consequences of those physical results. At the arm's maximum free-space limit of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_tcp_str`, even the transient impact model predicts `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_tcp_str`, exceeding the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_limit_str` criterion by a factor of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_ratio_mult_str`. Consequently, unseparated coworker proximity cannot be permitted at full free-space speed without additional physical containment. For a free hand that recoils upon impact, the criterion admits approach speeds up to `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`. At the chosen handover speed of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_str`, the model predicts a transient force of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_handover_str`, below the case criterion. If the coworker's hand is clamped against a rack upright or structural frame, however, the ceiling drops to `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_clamped_str`. At that same `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_str` approach speed, a clamped collision generates `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_handover_clamped_str`, which breaches the limit. The handover claim is therefore strictly a transient-contact claim, inheriting two premises: that the lumped-mass body model and effective mass accurately describe the collision, and that the handover geometry excludes pinching or clamping hazards. Because physical calculations alone cannot guarantee workspace clearance, the release case must establish both premises through empirical evidence and site inspection.

[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech]: **ISO/TS 15066 Values as Case Criteria**\index{ISO/TS 15066!case criterion}: The document supplies a body model and body-region force and pressure data for transient and quasi-static contact [@isots15066]. ISO 10218-2:2025 incorporates the collaborative-application requirements formerly published as ISO/TS 15066; ISO/TS 15066:2016 itself remains published and is under revision [@iso10218part2]. The `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_limit_str` handover criterion is none of those tabulated values and not an injury boundary; the site assessment chooses it for one body region, contact type, and geometry, so a change to any of the three reopens the claim instead of inheriting its margin.

Unlike the arm's instantaneous force criteria, the mobile base's claim is an integrated distance budget. Validating this claim requires empirical evidence bounding the perception observation age, communication bus latencies, and execution lease durations. @Sec-enforcement-composite-budget sized that budget term by term at aisle speed (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget), integrating @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope with the jerk-limited $\Glyph{C}^2$ braking profile from @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix, and found the spare and the reserve that dispatch-to-admission travel leaves. Release inherits those terms as premises. In deployment authorization, the critical engineering metric is the margin of clear distance that remains unspent, and the question release adds is how large an error in a single input would spend it. Notebook \ref{nbk-release-aisle-spare} recapitulates the enforcement budget and adds that question as step 4.

::: {#nbk-release-aisle-spare .callout-notebook title="The aisle spare"}

**Problem**: At the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, how much of the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance does the stopping budget leave unspent, what error in a single input would spend it, and how much remains once dispatch-to-admission work is charged?

**Variables**:

- Aisle speed $\SpeedAtDetection =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (Chosen); clear distance $\ClearDistance =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` (Illustrative, standing in for a site survey)
- Pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.tau_delay_str` (Derived from illustrative terms: `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_age_str` observation age plus `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_renewal_to_onset_str` from the last valid renewal to brake onset)
- Credible deceleration $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` (Illustrative) and jerk bound $\JerkLimit =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.j_brake_str` (Derived, @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
- Allowances $\LocalizationBound =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_loc_str` and $\TrackingErrorBound =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_track_str` (Illustrative); margin $\ProtectiveClearanceMargin =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_margin_str` (Chosen)
- Dispatch-to-admission allocation $\DispatchAdmissionInterval =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.delta_da_str` (Illustrative allocation, @sec-placement-dispatch-admission)

**Math**:

1. **Reaction**: $\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` $\times$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.tau_delay_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_reaction_str`.
2. **Braking**: Because $\SpeedAtDetection \ge \CredibleBrakingDeceleration^2/\JerkLimit$, the stop reaches full deceleration, and $\SpeedAtDetection^2/(2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration) + \SpeedAtDetection\,\CredibleBrakingDeceleration/(2\JerkLimit) =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_brake_quad_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_brake_jerk_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_braking_str`.
3. **Spare**: `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_reaction_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_braking_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_loc_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_track_str` $+$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_margin_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.budget_str`, leaving `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_mm_str` $-$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.budget_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str`.
4. **One input wrong**: As extra delay, `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str` $/$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_spare_str`. As weaker braking, setting step 2 equal to the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.braking_room_str` braking room gives $\BreakEvenBrakingDeceleration =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_break_even_str`, a `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_shortfall_pct_str` shortfall.
5. **Admission charged**: $\SpeedAtDetection\,\DispatchAdmissionInterval =$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` $\times$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.delta_da_str` $=$ `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.travel_da_str`, leaving a reserve of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.reserve_str`, or `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_reserve_str` at aisle speed.

**Result**: The budget spends all but `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str` of the clear distance before admission work, and all but `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.reserve_str` after it.

**Systems insight**: The validity of the stopping guarantee $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$ hinges on the narrow margin of unspent distance rather than the nominal distance consumed. Measured against the partial spare of step 3, a credible deceleration overstated by `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_shortfall_pct_str` spends the whole of it. The reserve that step 5 leaves after admission work is less than half that spare, so once $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ is charged a smaller braking error suffices.

:::

This reserve must also absorb any unmodeled runtime uncertainty, so it cannot be treated as extra allowable latency or repurposed as a margin for control handovers. The reserve left after admission work, `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_reserve_str` at aisle speed, tolerates less unbudgeted delay or braking shortfall than the break-even values of step 4. Unless each component of the timing and kinematic chain is measured, nothing shows that the reserve survives the latencies and friction variation of a production floor. Each of the three criteria (stop, latch, and handover) therefore depends directly on premises about achievable deceleration, sensor-to-actuator latency, and contact stiffness that no calculation can certify. Because these physical properties can degrade over mechanical operating life, an auditable safety case must expose these runtime dependencies so that certification engineers can judge whether the empirical evidence supports deployment.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_aisle_budget_spare_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One horizontal stacked bar in millimeters: reaction travel of 173.7 millimeters, braking of 605.3 millimeters, then allowances of 50 for localization, 40 for tracking, and 100 millimeters of physical margin, followed by a dashed box for the 131.0 millimeters spare that ends at a red line marking the 1.10 meters clear distance."}

*The partial budget leaves only `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str` of the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance spare.*
:::

## Safety Cases and Claims {#sec-release-safety-cases-claims}

A photograph of a clear aisle cannot establish that a loaded mobile base will stop before reaching an obstacle. A valid stopping claim depends on guaranteed physical clearance, actual braking capability, and end-to-end response timing, with each parameter supported by empirical evidence gathered under documented operating conditions. A safety case connects these physical premises to the release claim step by step, so an assessor can see which guarantees rest on measurements and which remain unverified assumptions.

### Claims, arguments, and warrants {#sec-release-assurance-grammar}

A bundle of test logs and benchmark plots gives a release reviewer no way to tell which physical claims the data actually support or where an unstated assumption hides. A safety case is auditable only when its logic is written down in a form that another engineer can inspect and challenge link by link. Two notations are widely used in practice, and both capture the same structure. The **claim-argument-evidence (CAE)**\index{Claim-argument-evidence!notation} framework divides the case into three parts. The *claim* is a statement about system behavior that is either true or false. The *argument* is the causal or inductive reasoning connecting the claim to retained support. The *evidence* consists of the calibrated measurements, justified analyses, and validated operating procedures [@bishop1998methodology; @bloomfield2014building]. **Goal Structuring Notation (GSN)**\index{Goal Structuring Notation!elements} draws the same structure as a directed graph: top-level goals (claims) split through explicit strategies (arguments) into concrete solutions (evidence items). Context and assumption nodes state the operating envelope within which each link holds [@kelly1998arguing; @kelly2004goal]. The fault injection records enter this graph directly as solutions supporting each named sub-claim. Because release adjudication turns an assurance graph into a binding operational authorization, the safety case of definition \ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!argument structure} evaluates directly to an enforceable release verdict.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The fault-record set, in which every record names the one release claim it supports, is established in @sec-verification-contract-matrix.
:::

This decomposition comes from Stephen Toulmin's model of practical argumentation[^fn-toulmin-argument-anatomy] [@toulmin1958uses]. In industrial practice, standards such as ANSI/UL 4600 require goal-based safety cases for autonomous physical products [@ul4600; @koopman2023ul4600]. Production autonomous fleets use this same structure. For example, Waymo organizes the safety case for its driverless ride-hailing operations around layered, dynamic claims showing the absence of unreasonable risk, arguing separately that its risk acceptance criteria are complete and that their empirical evaluation is sound [@favaro2023building]. For an embodied robot, the root claim $\AssuranceClaim_0$ states a testable physical invariant, such as a stopping distance inside the surveyed aisle clearance ($\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$) or a bounded collaborative contact force ($\CollaborativeContactForce \le \AssessedContactForceLimit$). Supporting sub-claims name the required mechanical, electrical, and computational conditions, and retained measurements, derivations, or validated procedures back each leaf. Writing these relationships as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) exposes intermediate dependencies and rules out circular reasoning, so a reviewer can trace any operational claim down to its physical measurements and operating assumptions.

[^fn-toulmin-argument-anatomy]: **Toulmin's Argument Anatomy**\index{Toulmin, Stephen!argument model}: *The Uses of Argument* [@toulmin1958uses] splits practical reasoning into claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, and rebuttal. Safety cases preserve this anatomy: evidence supplies the data, stated confidence acts as the qualifier, and the rebuttal becomes the defeater evaluated during adversarial review (@sec-release-adversarial-review).

::: {#dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case .callout-definition title="Claim-argument-evidence safety case"}

***Claim-argument-evidence safety case***\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!definition}\index{Safety case!physical AI} is a structured argument that a named machine, in a stated operating envelope and under a stated fault model, meets explicit physical criteria, written as claims that decompose through stated arguments into retained evidence.

1.  **Significance**: It makes a release decision checkable one link at a time. For the warehouse machine, the three inequalities of @eq-release-authorization-criterion become six claims whose leaves are individual premises. A reviewer can find the one premise, such as a braking deceleration no loaded trial has measured, on which the verdict turns.
2.  **Distinction**: A test report or benchmark score records what happened under the conditions sampled. A safety case states why that evidence supports a claim about conditions the machine has not yet met, and names the assumptions under which the reasoning stops holding.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that the case is paperwork assembled after development for a regulator. It is written with the design, and in this book's architecture its verdict decides what the permission path lets the machine do.

:::

The soundness of this argument DAG depends on keeping evidence distinct from demonstration. A **demonstration**\index{Demonstration!vs. evidence} records successful task execution across an uncharacterized test set, such as a string of clean door openings with the strike plate at its nominal position or a thousand collision-free warehouse runs. Demonstrations show nominal performance across observed runs, but they give no mathematical or statistical bounds on tail behavior, sensor faults, or corner cases outside those logged runs. Evidence, by contrast, consists of falsifiable, calibrated records with stated uncertainty bounds: an execution-time distribution measured on a hardware logic analyzer paired with worst-case execution time (WCET) bounds, loaded stopping trials across degraded friction surfaces, or hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) fault-injection traces at envelope corners. The evidence must match the scope of the claim. Nominal trials can support nominal capability claims, and calibration logs can validate sensor coordinate frames, but bounding an envelope limit or worst-case response requires systematic coverage, stated uncertainty margins, and an explicit warrant.

Connecting evidence to a claim requires a **warrant**\index{Warrant!inferential rule}, the reasoning principle that explains why the measured data support the claim. For a learned neural policy, teams often reach for an inductive warrant, arguing from thousands of failure-free test episodes to future operational reliability. The exposure wall analyzed in @sec-evaluation-limits shows why purely inductive warrants cannot support catastrophic hazard claims. At 95 percent confidence the zero-failure exposure wall of @eq-eval-exposure-wall becomes $\Time \ge 3.0/\ConstantHazardRate$ (because $\ln 20 \approx 3.0$), where $\ConstantHazardRate$ is the failure rate per operating hour to be demonstrated. Statistically proving an ultra-low failure rate of $10^{-9}$ per operating hour therefore requires billions of operating hours without a single failure [@butler1993infeasibility; @kalra2016driving]. Deciding what target rate is acceptable in the first place is an engineering and societal judgment that empirical testing cannot make on its own [@koopman2022how].

A sound safety case bridges this gap with deterministic architectural warrants. Rather than betting physical safety on policy generalization, the system grounds its top-level safety claims in an independent permission path. That path evaluates the control barrier functions of @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission to clamp actuator commands, and commands an assessed safe stop whenever a learned proposal approaches the boundary of the viable set $\ForwardInvariantSafeSet$. The architectural warrant narrows the claim rather than escaping physical limits. The permission path protects only against monitored hazards that the actuators can arrest within the available stopping clearance. The learned proposer still needs its own operational argument to show task capability and handle unmonitored tasks. Recent standards formalize these complementary roles. ISO/PAS 8800:2024 adapts automotive safety lifecycles, data curation rules, and assurance arguments to AI components [@iso8800]. The Assurance of Machine Learning in Autonomous Systems (AMLAS) framework supplies safety-case patterns for machine learning pipelines across autonomous systems [@hawkins2021amlas]. In this book's architecture, the permission path carries the safety argument for all monitored physical hazards. It anchors its formal claims to a rated watchdog and to the certified functions beneath it in the drives, the safety-rated laser scanner, and the arm's safety controller (@sec-release-standards-map). The learned proposer's argument can then focus on operational availability and unmonitored mission tasks.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How much an architectural shield's per-command guarantee dilutes into a system-level hazard rate is developed in @sec-frontier-shield-dilution.
:::

### Contextual assumptions and the weakest link {#sec-release-contextual-assumptions}

A stopping test passed on clean, dry concrete under bright warehouse lamps can fail the first time the robot enters a dim aisle if the safety case never stated the lighting assumption behind its camera exposure time. Every physical measurement rests on ambient conditions, and moving the machine into a dimly lit aisle can lengthen camera exposure and observation age even when the mechanical brakes and tires behave identically. An assurance argument must state these contextual assumptions explicitly so that measurements gathered under one set of conditions are never credited outside their verified operating envelope.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-low-light-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AN UNSTATED LIGHTING ASSUMPTION IN THE STOPPING BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (contextual-assumptions paragraph).
# │ Goal: Show how a lighting change the budget never named ages the navigation
# │       camera's image, and what it would cost the aisle budget's spare
# │       if the age check did not refuse the frames.
# │ Show: nominal and low-light exposure, the added observation age, the added
# │       travel at aisle speed, and its share of the spare.
# │ How: perception age is timed from mid-exposure (ObservationAgeModel), so a
# │      longer exposure adds half its increase
# │      (Scenarios.WarehouseNavCameraAgeAtAisleSpeed against ...DimAisle); spare
# │      from the finished budget Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_percent, check

class ReleaseLowLight:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and the two lighting cases ───────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
    AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
    NOMINAL = Scenarios.WarehouseNavCameraAgeAtAisleSpeed  # category: illustrative (nominal exposure)
    DIM = Scenarios.WarehouseNavCameraAgeDimAisle  # category: illustrative (a dim aisle doubles the exposure)
    STOP = Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed  # category: illustrative (finished budget at the aisle speed)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp_nominal = NOMINAL.exposure_time.to(millisecond)
    t_exp_low = DIM.exposure_time.to(millisecond)
    dt_age = (DIM.result.age - NOMINAL.result.age).to(millisecond)  # mid-exposure timestamp
    d_added = (DIM.result.age_travel - NOMINAL.result.age_travel).to(millimeter)
    spare = STOP.result.spare.to(millimeter)
    share_of_spare = (d_added / spare).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_exp_nominal.magnitude - 16.0) < 1e-9, "Navigation-camera exposure 16 ms")
    check(abs(dt_age.magnitude - 8.0) < 1e-9, "Low light adds 8 ms of observation age")
    check(abs(d_added.magnitude - 10.4) < 1e-9, "10.4 mm of added travel at 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(share_of_spare - 0.079) < 5e-3, "About 8 percent of the spare")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp_nominal_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_nominal, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_low_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_low, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dt_age_str = fmt_latency(dt_age, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_added_str = fmt_length(d_added, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    share_str = fmt_percent(round(share_of_spare * 100) / 100.0, precision=0, style="prose")
```

When an operating assumption is left unstated, safety depends entirely on whether a downstream check happens to catch the resulting deviation. In the mobile manipulator's stopping budget, the warrant quietly assumes that warehouse illumination permits the navigation camera to operate at its nominal exposure. If dim lighting doubles that exposure time from `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_nominal_str` to `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_low_str`, the observation arrives `{python} ReleaseLowLight.dt_age_str` older than assumed (measuring exposure age from mid-frame). Left unchecked, this additional latency translates to `{python} ReleaseLowLight.d_added_str` of extra travel at the robot's `{python} ReleaseLowLight.v_aisle_str` aisle velocity, consuming roughly `{python} ReleaseLowLight.share_str` of the budget's `{python} ReleaseLowLight.spare_str` margin. On this machine the permission path's frame admission age check, the freshness test of the observation contract (@sec-perception-observation-contract), rejects the delayed frames. Because an active chunk can execute only while its evidence and lease remain valid, the robot instead halts in an aisle where the design assumed it could run. The team meets the unstated lighting assumption as unexplained availability loss rather than as a collision, and what kept the blind spot from eroding clearance was a latency check that knows nothing about illumination. A design without that check would have spent the margin silently.

Assumptions that lack runtime monitors carry far greater danger. Mechanical drift in a camera mount can introduce steady-state calibration offsets while every frame passes freshness and timestamp validations. The safety case must explicitly link localization tolerances to calibration routines and physical inspection logs. Treating fresh telemetry as proof of accurate spatial calibration leaves that warrant unsupported.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Premises that no sensor on the machine can observe, and the restrictions they force on a release claim, are developed in @sec-frontier-method-limits.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-argument-confidence
#| echo: false
```
