```{python}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HOW CONFIDENCE COMBINES IN A SAFETY ARGUMENT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-contextual-assumptions (the conjunctive and
# │          multi-legged argument paragraphs).
# │ Goal: Show that doubt accumulates across required premises, and that two
# │       independent legs can support a claim better than either leg alone.
# │ Show: confidence in a conjunction of n required premises; confidence in a
# │       claim supported by either of two independent legs.
# │ How: Scenarios.SafetyArgumentConfidence: independent premises, conjunction
# │      = product of confidences (calc_conjunctive_confidence); two independent
# │      legs fail together with probability (1-p1)(1-p2)
# │      (calc_multilegged_confidence).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Scenarios
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check

class ReleaseArgumentConfidence:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: a stipulated argument (a teaching illustration, not a machine value)
    ARG = Scenarios.SafetyArgumentConfidence  # category: illustrative (stipulated confidences)
    p_premise = ARG.premise_confidence  # category: illustrative (confidence in each required premise)
    n_premises = ARG.premises  # category: illustrative (number of required premises)
    p_leg = ARG.leg_confidence  # category: illustrative (confidence in each of two independent legs)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    p_conjunction = ARG.conjunction
    p_two_legs = ARG.multilegged

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(p_conjunction - 0.904) < 5e-4, "Ten premises at 0.99 give about 0.90")
    check(p_conjunction < p_premise, "The conjunction is weaker than its weakest premise")
    check(abs(p_two_legs - 0.99) < 1e-9, "Two independent legs at 0.90 give 0.99")
    check(p_two_legs > p_leg, "Independent legs support the claim better than either leg")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    p_premise_str = fmt(p_premise, precision=2)
    n_premises_str = fmt(n_premises, precision=0)
    p_conjunction_str = fmt(round(p_conjunction, 2), precision=2)
    p_leg_str = fmt(p_leg, precision=2)
    p_two_legs_str = fmt(round(p_two_legs, 2), precision=2)
```

A safety case is not an aggregate scorecard in which high performance in one branch compensates for a deficit in another. Benchmark accuracy on an object recognition dataset cannot offset an uncharacterized latency tail on a CAN FD (Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate) bus, nor can millions of simulated training episodes compensate for missing brake-wear measurements. When every child claim is *required*, the argument is conjunctive, and it is no stronger than its weakest required premise. In practice it is usually weaker, because doubt across independent premises accumulates. For a stipulated probability model, let each event mean that one required premise is valid under its stated conditions, and let $\RequiredPremiseConfidence_1, \dots, \RequiredPremiseConfidence_n$ be the assigned event probabilities. These are not finite-trial confidence levels and estimate neither this robot's measured hazard rate nor calibrated assurance confidence. Define the illustrative claim event $\AssuranceClaim$ exactly as the conjunction of these independent events; its probability is their product:
$$\Pr(\AssuranceClaim) = \prod_{i=1}^{\RequiredPremiseCount} \RequiredPremiseConfidence_i.$$ {#eq-release-conjunctive-confidence}

If each of `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.n_premises_str` required premises holds with assigned probability `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_premise_str`, the conjunction holds with only about `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_conjunction_str`, lower than any individual premise. The mobile base's stopping claim is conjunctive in exactly this way. Surveyed clear distance, credible braking deceleration, brake onset latency, observation age, and localization and tracking tolerances all enter a single stopping budget. A flawed warrant in any single term invalidates the root claim, regardless of how thoroughly the other terms are documented. An assessor therefore looks to the least supported required premise and the number of premises sharing the claim, not to the gross volume of supporting documentation.

This conjunctive degradation has one principled engineering exception. An argument can support a claim through two *independent* legs, either of which suffices on its own, so that the claim fails only if both legs fail simultaneously [@bloomfield2003multilegged]. In a separate stipulated model, define $\AssuranceClaim$ exactly as the union of $\ArgumentLegCount$ independent sufficient-leg events with assigned probabilities $\ArgumentLegConfidence_1, \dots, \ArgumentLegConfidence_{\ArgumentLegCount}$. The event holds unless all legs fail:
$$\Pr(\AssuranceClaim) = 1 - \prod_{j=1}^{\ArgumentLegCount} (1 - \ArgumentLegConfidence_j).$$ {#eq-release-multilegged-confidence}

If each of two independent legs holds with assigned probability `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_leg_str`, the combined claim holds with roughly `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_two_legs_str`, well above either leg alone. The equality describes the stipulated event model. If sufficient-leg events merely imply a broader physical claim, their union probability supplies a lower bound rather than automatically equaling the probability of that claim. The third law, *proposal is not permission*, instead supplies a conditional architectural argument: a policy error alone cannot breach a monitored stopping or contact invariant while the qualified enforcer, plant, sensing, timing, and fault premises hold. Policy validation and per-tick permission checks together do not justify assigning independent probabilities to their success.[^fn-diverse-legs-independence] Claim C5 in @tbl-16-cae-scorecard requires evidence that shared processors, memory buses, power rails, or sensor pipelines cannot compromise the permission path under the credited fault and interference model. Such isolation evidence addresses common causes within its qualified scope; it does not alone establish every statistical independence assumption. If the event independence is unsupported, the two-leg probability calculation is unavailable; shared causes must be represented explicitly in the argument. The enforcer leg is itself conjunctive across its own physical premises, because claims C1 through C4 must all hold for the enforcer to function. Diverse legs protect against policy failure; they cannot make up for unmeasured brake physics or missing timing margins, so the reviewer must check every leaf against the actual plant.

[^fn-diverse-legs-independence]: **Independence of Diverse Legs**\index{Design diversity!common-mode failure}: When independently written versions of a software specification were evaluated on identical inputs, they failed coincidentally far more frequently than independent failure models predicted, statistically rejecting the independence assumption [@knight1986experimental]. Design diversity does not by itself yield independence in failure.

### Matching the argument to the machine {#sec-release-argument-plant-alignment}

Flawless arithmetic on assumed braking and latency numbers proves only that the robot would stop in time if the numbers were true; it says nothing about whether the physical machine on the floor actually meets them. While analytical stopping models relate brake onset, deceleration, sensor age, and tracking error cleanly on paper, an equation is only as sound as its physical inputs. A release reviewer must check which parameters come from measurements on the production hardware and which remain unverified design assumptions.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-claims
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE SIX RELEASE CLAIMS ON THE RUNNING MACHINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (scorecard lead-in) and
# │          @tbl-16-cae-scorecard.
# │ Goal: Instance claims C1-C6 on the warehouse mobile manipulator.
# │ Show: base budget at aisle speed against the clear distance; latch force at
# │       brake command, remaining compression, and the arm stop it requires;
# │       mug pick and handover speeds with the handover ceiling and force;
# │       renewal-to-onset time; enforcer WCET and deadline; friction needed
# │       for a_brake; observation age; the handover deadline T_latest at the
# │       in-loop takeover slow-down and at aisle speed.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; the finished budget
# │      Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed (jerk-limited S-curve stop,
# │      jerk bound = the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit);
# │      the takeover budget at the in-loop slow-down
# │      (Scenarios.WarehouseInLoopTakeoverAtRequestSpeed); latch and handover
# │      contact premises from EnforcementContactForce
# │      (calc-release-contact-premises).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_force, fmt_mass, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
from mlsysim.physics.drivetrain import calc_required_friction

class ReleaseClaims:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
    AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
    STOP = Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed  # category: illustrative (finished budget at the aisle speed)
    TAKEOVER = Scenarios.WarehouseInLoopTakeoverAtRequestSpeed  # category: illustrative (in-loop takeover slow-down)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE: one warrant quantity per claim ────────────────────────────────
    # C1 base: finished budget at aisle speed.
    budget_aisle = STOP.result.required_distance.to(millimeter)
    spare_aisle = STOP.result.spare.to(millimeter)
    # C1 door: force at brake command and the arm stop that keeps it under the limit.
    f_cmd = EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd
    x_remaining = EnforcementContactForce.x_rem
    a_arm_needed = EnforcementContactForce.a_arm
    # C1 handover: transient (free-hand) force at the handover speed, ISO hand body model.
    f_handover = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover
    # C2: last valid renewal to brake onset.
    t_renewal_to_onset = Scenarios.WarehouseRenewalReferencedStop.delay.to(millisecond)
    # C3: optimistic friction floor with all weight on driven wheels; qualify actual loaded stops.
    mu_min = calc_required_friction(AISLE.a_brake)
    v_handover_ceiling = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling
    # C6: an unacknowledged handover falls back by the spare spent as time, at the
    # preliminary in-loop takeover slow-down and at aisle speed (a policy request).
    t_timeout = STOP.result.delay_spare.to(millisecond)
    spare_takeover = TAKEOVER.result.machine.spare.to(millimeter)
    t_latest_takeover = TAKEOVER.result.deadline.to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the table ────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 968.9925) < 5e-3, "C1 base budget at 1.3 m/s")
    check(budget_aisle < AISLE.d_clear, "C1 budget fits inside the clear distance")
    check(abs(f_cmd.magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "C1 latch force at brake command")
    check(abs(x_remaining.magnitude - 0.1525) < 1e-6, "C1 remaining compression 0.15 mm")
    check(abs(a_arm_needed.magnitude - 2.95) < 0.005, "C1 arm stop premise about 3 m/s^2 (computed 2.95)")
    check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "C1 transient handover force 20.7 N")
    check(f_handover < AISLE.f_contact_criterion, "C1 handover force under the criterion")
    check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "C2 renewal-to-onset 82 ms")
    check(AISLE.enforcer_wcet < AISLE.enforcer_deadline < AISLE.t_tick, "C2 WCET < deadline < tick")
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "C3 friction floor 0.204")
    check(abs(AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-9, "C4 age 51.6 ms")
    check(abs(t_timeout.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, "C6 fallback by 100.8 ms at 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(spare_takeover.magnitude - 563.71) < 0.05, "C6 spare 563.7 mm at the 0.75 m/s slow-down")
    check(abs(t_latest_takeover.magnitude - 751.6) < 0.05, "C6 fallback by 751.6 ms at 0.75 m/s")
    check(abs(RM.tcp_speed_limit.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "C1 mug pick under the 1.0 m/s TCP limit")
    check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "C1 transient handover ceiling 0.24 m/s")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_cmd_str = fmt_force(f_cmd, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_remaining.magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm_needed.magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_handover, precision=1)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.perception_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_timeout_str = fmt_latency(round(t_timeout.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_latest_takeover_str = fmt_latency(round(t_latest_takeover.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)

# Module-level exports for downstream cells and figure guards
budget_aisle = ReleaseClaims.budget_aisle
spare_aisle = ReleaseClaims.spare_aisle
f_cmd = ReleaseClaims.f_cmd
x_remaining = ReleaseClaims.x_remaining
a_arm_needed = ReleaseClaims.a_arm_needed
f_handover = ReleaseClaims.f_handover
t_renewal_to_onset = ReleaseClaims.t_renewal_to_onset
mu_min = ReleaseClaims.mu_min
```

For collaborative manipulation tasks, biomechanical thresholds govern the contact force argument once the claim explicitly details the target body region, contact classification (transient vs. quasi-static), pressure distribution, impact geometry, and measurement methodology [@iso10218part2]. The mobile base's claims, which form the core of the release argument, derive directly from empirical stopping distance budgets and site survey logs. Two conceptual frameworks borrowed from automotive engineering organize the fault analysis. Functional safety mitigates hazards arising from hardware malfunctions or systematic software defects [@iso26262]. In contrast, Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF) addresses hazards stemming from performance insufficiencies or specification gaps in the absence of hardware faults, such as an obstacle detector failing to recognize a worker partially obscured by shrink-wrapped pallet staging [@iso21448]. Every leaf of the release argument requires support appropriate to its premise: qualified plant and timing observations, justified analysis, or validated operating restrictions under explicit assumptions. The formal standards governing these subsystems are machinery safety standards, mapped in @sec-release-standards-map to each component.

The claim-argument-evidence scorecard in @tbl-16-cae-scorecard defines six core release claims, pairing each physical warrant with its adjudication against the evidence developed in this book. Claim C3 shows how a warrant fails. An unnoticed oil slick on a polished concrete floor destroys wheel traction and invalidates the nominal deceleration model. A physically realizable condition that invalidates an assurance warrant in this manner is a **defeater**\index{Defeaters!definition} [@goodenough2013eliminative]. Adversarial safety review hunts for these defeaters (@sec-release-adversarial-review). Similarly, Claim C6 depends strictly on test records validating the four supervisory authority handoff rules (A1–A4) established in @sec-intervention-evidence-tuples. Drawn as an assurance DAG (@fig-16-argument-graph), the argument splits C1 into its three physical scenarios (base stop, door latch, mug handover), ends every branch in a premise leaf whose outline records the maturity of its evidence, and attaches the oil-film defeater directly to C3. Because no leaf has been measured on the loaded production configuration, every row of the scorecard evaluates to `REFUSE`, the verdict that grants no operating permit and commands an assessed stop or hold (@sec-release-three-verdicts). @Sec-release-case-worked-full works through why, branch by branch.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-argument-graph-guard
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ARGUMENT GRAPH LABELS (FIGURE GUARD)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-16-argument-graph (fig16_argument_graph.svg)

# │ Goal: Keep the hand-drawn premise leaves in step with calc-release-claims.
# │ Show: 969.0 mm budget, 131.0 mm spare, 39 N latch force, 0.15 mm, 3 m/s^2,
# │       20.7 N handover force, 82 ms renewal-to-onset, 250/400 µs WCET and
# │       deadline, mu 0.204 and 0.60, 51.6 ms age.
# │ How: format the scenario and ReleaseClaims quantities and require each
# │      label string in the SVG.
# │

# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import os as _os
from mlsysim.fmt import check

_svg_rel = "images/svg/fig16_argument_graph.svg"
_svg_path = next(_p for _p in (_svg_rel, "books/vol4/16_release/" + _svg_rel, "vol4/16_release/" + _svg_rel) if _os.path.exists(_p))
with open(_svg_path) as _f:
    _svg = _f.read()

_labels = [
    f"{budget_aisle.magnitude:.1f} mm of {AISLE.d_clear.to(meter).magnitude:.2f} m clear",
    f"spare {spare_aisle.magnitude:.1f} mm at {AISLE.v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude:.1f} m/s",
    f"{AISLE.a_brake.to(meter / second**2).magnitude:.0f} m/s², onset {AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond).magnitude:.0f} ms",
    f"tracking {AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude:.0f} mm, local. {AISLE.delta_loc.to(millimeter).magnitude:.0f} mm",
    f"{f_cmd.to(newton).magnitude:.0f} N at onset ≤ {AISLE.f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude:.0f} N",
    f"latch, guarded {AISLE.v_latch_approach.to(meter / second).magnitude:.2f} m/s",
    f"arm stops within {x_remaining.to(millimeter).magnitude:.2f} mm",
    f"needs about {a_arm_needed.to(meter / second**2).magnitude:.0f} m/s²",
    f"{f_handover.magnitude:.1f} N ≤ {AISLE.f_contact_criterion.to(newton).magnitude:.0f} N at {AISLE.v_handover.to(meter / second).magnitude:.2f} m/s",
    f"onset ≤ {t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude:.0f} ms after renewal",
    f"WCET {AISLE.enforcer_wcet.to(microsecond).magnitude:.0f} µs &lt; {AISLE.enforcer_deadline.to(microsecond).magnitude:.0f} µs",
    f"floor μ ≥ {mu_min:.3f}, every aisle",
    f"dry-floor survey value {AISLE.mu_dry:.2f}",
    f"dispatch age {AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond).magnitude:.1f} ms",
]
for _lab in _labels:
    check(_lab in _svg, f"argument graph label is stale or missing: {_lab}")
```

: **Claim-argument-evidence review for the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Six claims and their adjudication on this book's evidence. Displayed stopping distances and waiting allowances are partial calculations; admission work, physical response, and required reserve must be charged at their own events. A failed or unknown branch cannot be compensated by nominal model accuracy. {#tbl-16-cae-scorecard tbl-colwidths="[14,58,28]"}

::: {#chk-release-claim-argument-evidence-and-inductive-warrants .callout-checkpoint title="Safety case decomposition and warrants"}

Before presenting a safety case for adjudication, test its structure:

- [ ] **Top-level claim falsifiability**: Can you state the top-level claim as a falsifiable physical proposition, such as a stop inside the clear distance, rather than an aspiration?
- [ ] **Warrant validity**: Can you name the warrant connecting each test bench to the claim above it, and the premises under which that warrant holds?
- [ ] **Defeater enumeration**: Can you show where a defeater such as lens fouling or bus arbitration collisions appears in the argument graph?
- [ ] **Evidentiary provenance**: Can you trace each empirical evidence node to its signed test trace and current calibration, and each analytical or procedural node to its retained derivation, assumptions, or accountable procedure and validation?
:::

The scorecard enforces a strict separation between physical safety requirements and the empirical records available to substantiate them. Even when every internal warrant is traced to a hardware measurement, however, an engineering team does not choose its own risk-reduction hierarchy or protective ratings in a vacuum. The release reviewer must keep this evidentiary discipline across the entire assurance tree while verifying which external machinery and regulatory standards govern each branch.

### The standards map for the running machine {#sec-release-standards-map}

Certifying an industrial mobile manipulator against road-vehicle standards, or against fixed-arm standards that ignore a moving base, leaves the hazards of a moving arm on a moving base uncovered. Before authorizing deployment, an assessor must establish which formal standards and regulations govern each subsystem and verify where the corresponding evidence was gathered. Because this running machine is an industrial mobile manipulator rather than an autonomous road vehicle, its formal certification path follows industrial machinery directives rather than automotive standards. ISO 12100 sets the overall risk-management framework. The engineering team identifies hazards, evaluates risk, and applies a three-step reduction hierarchy, with inherently safe design first, engineered safeguards second, and user warnings and operating procedures last [@iso12100]. Every standard in @tbl-16-standards-map addresses a specific tier of this hierarchy. Autonomy and automotive standards enter as borrowed engineering methods, supplying vocabulary for learned policies, distribution shifts, and assurance cases that traditional industrial standards are only beginning to adopt.

| Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 [@eu2024cra]                   | Applies from 11 December 2027 | Cyber Resilience Act: cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, vulnerability handling, security updates                                                                                                                               | The update channel, the signed images, and the fleet's vulnerability reports                                                     | @sec-release-modular-safety-cases                                                                           |

: **Standards map for the warehouse mobile manipulator (as of 2026)**: Each document, its edition, what it governs, the part of the running machine it covers, and the section that produces the evidence it asks for. Machinery standards form the certification route; the road-vehicle and autonomy documents are borrowed method. Editions and dates change; a later printing should refresh this table. {#tbl-16-standards-map tbl-colwidths="[17,13,28,24,18]"}

Two standards in the map require a clear boundary because the running machine straddles mobile robotics and fixed manipulation. ISO 10218-2:2025 governs industrial robot systems and collaborative work cells, but it explicitly excludes the kinetic hazards introduced when a manipulator rides on a mobile platform [@iso10218part2], which is this warehouse machine's configuration. Conversely, ISO 3691-4 treats the mobile base as a driverless industrial truck. The standard that bridges this gap by treating the mobile manipulator as a single unit is ANSI/A3 R15.08. Mounting an active manipulator on a mobile platform classifies the machine as an Industrial Mobile Robot (IMR) Type C, and Part 2 sets the safety requirements for integrating that combined unit into an active facility [@ansi1508part1; @ansi1508part2]. In jurisdictions where R15.08 lacks statutory standing, the combined hazards of mobility and manipulation fall back onto the machine's primary ISO 12100 risk assessment.

A second boundary concerns which layers of the permission path carry formal safety ratings. As @sec-enforcement-certified-functions established, the only rated function within the permission path is the safety MCU's lease-expiry and heartbeat watchdog, which asserts Safe Torque Off (STO) or Safe Stop 1 (SS1) on the motor drives when valid renewals cease. The admission checks that evaluate neural proposals carry no rating. The certified functions of the motor drives, the safety-rated laser scanner, and the arm's safety controller sit beneath the permission path. For release, the formal protective claims for every monitored hazard therefore rest on that watchdog and that certified layer. The release argument still uses the software admission checks for operational utility and nominal hazard prevention, but any hazard claim that depends only on unrated software remains an empirical premise rather than a certified safety function.

Statutory compliance reaches physical AI through product-safety law rather than through standalone artificial intelligence rules, and its sharpest consequence for release concerns updates. Under the European Union's Machinery Regulation [@eu2023machinery], a *substantial modification*\index{Substantial modification!Machinery Regulation} is any physical or digital change made after deployment that the original manufacturer did not foresee and that introduces a new hazard or raises an existing risk enough to require additional safeguarding. An organization that pushes an unverified over-the-air model update can therefore become, in law, the manufacturer of the modified machine, with every obligation that role carries (@sec-release-modular-safety-cases). The same regulation requires third-party conformity assessment[^fn-conformity-assessment-route] for machinery whose safety components have fully or partially self-evolving behavior and use machine learning to execute safety functions, so a learned safety function cannot be self-certified. Its essential requirements also constrain learning directly. The limits of each safety function must be documented in the manufacturer's risk assessment. No rule or parameter the machine generates, even during a learning phase, may change those limits where the change could create a hazardous situation (Annex III, section 1.2.1). Keeping the learned proposer outside the permission path meets that requirement only if the safety argument does not depend on the proposer's learned behavior. Two neighboring acts reach the same machine. The EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 [@eu2024aiact], as amended in July 2026 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 [@eu2026omnibus], places the Machinery Regulation in Section B of its Annex I, so AI-specific safety rules for machines arrive through the machinery framework. The Commission must adopt delegated acts that insert those rules into the Machinery Regulation's Annex III and that apply by 2 August 2028. Because the robot receives network updates, it is also a product with digital elements under the Cyber Resilience Act [@eu2024cra], which requires vulnerability handling and secure updates throughout the manufacturer's support period, at least five years unless the product is expected to be in use for less. Its duty to report actively exploited vulnerabilities applies from 11 September 2026, ahead of the rest of the act. @Tbl-16-standards-map lists the dates from which the other obligations apply. These milestones do not alter the underlying physics or systems engineering; they set the calendar dates by which statutory authorities will demand an inspectable assurance case.

[^fn-conformity-assessment-route]: **Conformity Assessment**\index{Conformity assessment!Machinery Regulation}: The formal procedure through which a manufacturer certifies that a machine fulfills all essential health and safety requirements before affixing the CE marking [@eu2023machinery]. While manufacturers may self-assess conventional machinery, high-risk systems and self-evolving AI safety components require third-party evaluation by a notified body. Because the conformity assessment path is fixed before market entry, every record in the release manifest must be formatted for independent inspection.

The standards map also marks the boundary between statutory obligations and the systems architecture developed in this book. Formal standards prescribe documented arguments, rated protective functions, and independent third-party assessments. The verdicts, signed capability descriptors, and release manifest developed in the rest of this chapter are one engineering architecture for carrying those obligations into the runtime system. The safety case accepted before deployment then stays binding on the machine long after the inspectors have left the floor.

## The Three Verdicts {#sec-release-three-verdicts}

Treating a release sign-off as an informal paper memo forces teams either to ground a useful machine over an unmeasured corner case or to wave it onto the floor with unproven assumptions. Every row of @tbl-16-cae-scorecard ends in an adjudication, and the release decision resolves the entire assertion DAG into one of three verdicts: **unconditional operation**\index{Verdicts!unconditional operation}, **conditional operation**\index{Verdicts!conditional operation}, or **refusal to operate**\index{Verdicts!refusal to operate}. In this book's architecture, these verdicts are cryptographically signed capability descriptors loaded into the real-time safety microcontroller before motor power stages are energized, not advisory certificates or administrative paperwork. A valid descriptor is the machine's **operating permit**\index{Operating permit!definition}: while it holds, the permission path may admit the policy's tracking commands inside the envelope the descriptor names, and when it is revoked or absent, the permission path admits none. Although safety standards do not mandate this specific mechanism (@sec-release-standards-map), the qualified gate and permission path enforce the authenticated descriptor's limits on physical operation. The first verdict, unconditional operation (`UNCOND`), authorizes tracking proposals across the full operating envelope specified in a signed release manifest, provided its standing conditions remain continuously verified. Each hazard claim in that safety case requires qualified measurements, justified analysis, or validated operating restrictions applicable to the specified physical plant, payload distribution, operational design domain, and fault set. Brake thermal capacity, stopping clearance, and tracking-error bounds must all be qualified for that envelope, and independent permission checks must stand wherever learned policy proposals can reach physical actuators. The verdict does not eliminate residual or newly emergent hazards; it authorizes operation solely under the assessed claims and requires detection and safe withdrawal within the qualified response budget whenever a physical premise fails.

::: {#dfn-release-verdict .callout-definition title="Release verdict"}

***Release verdict***\index{Release verdict!definition} is the signed decision that sets how much authority a named machine's permission path may grant: `UNCOND` for the full assessed operating envelope, `COND` for a separately evidenced restricted envelope, or `REFUSE` when any required premise is missing, contradicted, or unknown, in each case only while its standing conditions hold.

1.  **Significance**: It turns the weakest premise of the argument into the machine's operating limit on $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$. On this book's illustrative evidence every claim carries an unknown premise, so the warehouse machine's verdict is `REFUSE`. A stipulated set of loaded stopping and floor records would support a `COND` at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str` on inspected floors, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` optimistic all-weight partial ceiling.
2.  **Distinction**: A test result records the outcome of an individual trial, whereas a degraded mode is an autonomous runtime fallback triggered during execution. By contrast, a release verdict is established before deployment: it names the qualified envelope and the empirical evidence upon which it rests, while leaving the proposal boundary fixed, since the permission path continues to validate every proposed action individually.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A common misconception is that a conditional verdict (`COND`) can patch an incomplete safety case by ignoring an unproven claim. A restricted envelope instead demands its own dedicated evidence and analytical limits; an unresolved premise in the primary case leaves that operating mode firmly refused.

:::

### Restricted operation and access boundaries {#sec-release-verdicts-ssm}

When a safety case lacks evidence for full-speed aisle travel or open-floor contact, letting the robot run under an informal operating note leaves the permission path enforcing the wrong limits. The second verdict, conditional operation (`COND`), applies when empirical evidence supports the stated hazard claims within a restricted subset of the envelope and binds the permission path to those narrower limits. In the running machine, `COND` selects a pre-validated safety configuration, much like industrial safety controllers and protective optical scanners switch between pre-validated field sets[^fn-scanner-field-sets] and speed-monitoring profiles. All restricted kinematic thresholds ($\SpeedBound \le \RestrictedSpeedBound$, $\ProfileAccelerationBound \le \RestrictedAccelerationBound$) and spatial geofences are evaluated and validated as one configuration before release; the runtime verdict selects among these vetted profiles rather than inventing parameters on the fly. A conditional verdict (`COND`) is an offline, predeployment contract that restricts the machine's operating envelope until re-adjudication. A **degraded mode**\index{Degraded mode!definition} is an online runtime fallback, pre-assessed and named in the signed release, that the permission path invokes when an active subsystem loses telemetry or sensor redundancy (@sec-release-blind-travel-limits sizes one for the base). Release then enforces physical, kinematic, or environmental boundaries that exclude unverified hazard states, such as de-rated joint speeds, a restricted illumination range, or a physical barrier that keeps humans outside the manipulator's workspace. Where contact force cannot be bounded for unseparated co-presence, a restricted release case may require physical separation: @fig-16-real-robot-safety-cell illustrates yellow perimeter mesh fencing around an industrial workcell. Crediting that separation requires validated access-interlock and stopping evidence showing that the protective response completes before hazardous access.

[^fn-scanner-field-sets]: **Safety Scanner Field Sets**\index{Safety laser scanner!field sets}: A safety laser scanner stores several protective-field geometries that were configured and validated in advance, and a safety controller selects one of them from encoded speed or position inputs. The scanner never computes a new field at runtime. `COND` borrows the pattern, so the verdict selects a pre-assessed limit set and no untested parameter can reach the permission path.

::: {#fig-16-real-robot-safety-cell fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Physical separation example**: A yellow industrial arm works behind yellow mesh fencing. Fencing can be one condition of a restricted release when a validated access interlock and stopping test support it. (Photo: PEO ACWA, Pueblo Chemical Agent-Destruction Pilot Plant, 2012, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pueblo_Chemical_Agent-Destruction_Pilot_Plant_Robotic_Operating_Area_(8456400290).jpg), [CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/).)" fig-alt="Yellow industrial robot arm and metal equipment inside a factory bay bounded by yellow mesh fence panels and gates. A blue lift is outside the foreground fence. Wiring, interlock rating, and stopping behavior are not visible."}
![](images/jpg/fig16_real_robot_safety_cell.jpg){width="85%" fig-alt="Yellow industrial robot arm and metal equipment inside a factory bay bounded by yellow mesh fence panels and gates. A blue lift is outside the foreground fence. Wiring, interlock rating, and stopping behavior are not visible."}
:::

Fencing excludes unseparated contact by keeping people out of the hazardous volume. The alternative that lets people share the floor, speed and separation monitoring (SSM, @sec-enforcement-certified-functions), needs a different access claim from the stationary-person stopping claim of C1. Its separation clearance must account for human approach velocity across both system reaction time and physical deceleration, robot displacement before brake onset, the executed braking profile, and measurement uncertainty. The warehouse case retains its site crossing rule; engineering teams cannot substitute a stationary-person stopping model into this context and claim to have achieved unseparated, open-floor human-robot collaboration.

Every quantitative condition attached to a release verdict names the operational limit the permission path enforces, maintaining explicit margin below the calculated physical ceiling. Item handover illustrates this margin requirement. The contract signs a TCP\index{Tool center point!handover speed contract} speed below the absolute ceiling that the contact criterion admits under @eq-release-unbraked-force. The gap between these two speeds accounts for unobserved physical evolution between discrete sensor samples: velocity growth between sampling instants, encoder quantization noise, and drive lag during an enforcement clamp. A contract signed at the theoretical ceiling leaves zero margin for these physical latency terms, and the release case requires measured empirical bounds on each term before the signed operational speed can be accepted.

The inspected-floor condition follows the same discipline. Where the site inspection regime certifies a friction coefficient of only `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`, the illustrative all-weight-on-driven-wheels screen uses the optimistic traction ceiling $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \Gravity =$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str` $\times$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.g_str` $=$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.a_inspected_str` against the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.a_brake_str` that the dry-floor budget assumes. Actual loaded credible deceleration also depends on the driven-wheel load share, drive and geometry conditions, and qualified stopping traces. Under the all-weight screening premise, the partial budget that admits `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling_str` on surveyed floors admits only `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` under this reduced traction. Visual inspection alone cannot establish this lower friction bound because a thin film of transparent oil readily escapes visual detection. The site must qualify both the friction assessment method and the operating procedures (cleaning schedules, spill isolation, and access restrictions) that preserve the assessed floor state between inspections. If that maintenance regime cannot guarantee the exclusion of contaminants over the authorized operating interval, reducing vehicle speed does not salvage the safety case; the aisle remains refused.

The third verdict, refusal to operate (`REFUSE`), is mandatory whenever the safety case has missing warrants, uncharacterized tail latencies, incomplete fault-injection coverage, or unmonitored failure modes. For systems where torque removal causes immediate physical harm (such as upright bipedal humanoids falling under gravity), `REFUSE` cannot simply de-energize motor phases to zero torque; it must execute an assessed, powered descent or seated hold. If the safety enforcer's worst-case execution time under the designated computational placement has never been verified against its `{python} ReleaseClaims.deadline_str` deadline, or if the fault-injection campaign omitted common-cause failures identified in the deployment topology, the hazard remains unquantified and cannot support release. Refusal is likewise mandatory whenever physical measurements contradict the mathematical model behind a safety budget term, such as loaded stopping trials that yield decelerations below the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` assumed by the braking model.

A refusal verdict is an actionable engineering result rather than an administrative dead end. It redirects schedule pressure toward evidence by pointing to the exact broken link in the assertion DAG. If release is refused because loaded stopping trials contradict the braking model, the engineering team does not debate risk tolerance. Developers instead repeat physical braking trials at maximum payload mass until the qualified trial campaign and its uncertainty analysis support a credible lower deceleration bound. They then re-derive the stopping budget from that lower bound and submit for re-adjudication only when the aisle budget closes on validated data. The refusal verdict names the exact empirical test that must pass before re-adjudication can proceed.

Accountability for the release decision must rest with a named **lead systems adjudicator**\index{Lead systems adjudicator!accountability} rather than being split across development teams. When a vision team signs off on perception metrics, an actuator supplier on torque ratings, and a machine learning team on policy convergence, each group can assume that another layer holds the safety margin. The lead adjudicator alone attests that the integrated, physical machine satisfies the safety case. This sign-off binds the release verdict to a specific set of technical records: cryptographic digests of verified policy weights, calibration logs for manipulator contact-force sensing, empirical brake-onset measurements paired with justified worst-case response bounds, and fully loaded stopping trials establishing credible deceleration limits. The adjudicator signs the release manifest with a private key held inside a hardware security module,[^fn-hsm-release-signing] binding the manifest to the organization's signing key and sign-off record. The robot runtime checks this digital signature against a public key anchored in its hardware root of trust before enabling actuators.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The adjudicator's signature as one of several decisions behind each admitted action, each needing a named owner, is developed in @sec-responsibility-many-hands.
:::

[^fn-hsm-release-signing]: **Hardware Security Module (HSM)**\index{Hardware security module!release signing}: A tamper-resistant device can generate and retain a non-exportable private key and perform signing inside its own boundary. The signature identifies the signing key; authenticated access, sign-off records, and key-custody controls establish who authorized its use.

The adjudicator's signature records the internal acceptance of the engineering organization, whereas external certification requires independent evaluation. UL 4600 requires independent assessment of the autonomous safety case [@ul4600], and machinery whose primary safety functions rely on machine learning falls under regulations, such as the European Union Machinery Regulation, that require third-party conformity assessment (@sec-release-standards-map). An assessor who did not build the safety case brings an independent view to the assumptions that shaped its trade-offs. Organizational separation alone does not establish a probability of coincident error or the statistical independence required by @eq-release-multilegged-confidence. The release manifest must therefore retain the full body of raw physical evidence needed for an independent audit, not just the final verdict.

The adjudicator ultimately signs one of the three decisions summarized in @tbl-16-verdicts-taxonomy. A conditional verdict requires its own independently evidenced restricted envelope; an unresolved gap in the nominal argument cannot be relabeled as an operational constraint. No verdict ever moves the proposal boundary. Under both `UNCOND` and `COND`, learned policies only propose candidate actions while the deterministic safety enforcer independently admits or blocks every control command, as principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission} requires. The release verdict sets the physical envelope that the permission path enforces; it never grants learned policies unchecked authority.

| Signed verdict | Evidence required                                                                                                | Permission and runtime limits                                                                                             | Expiry or refusal trigger                                       |
|:---------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `UNCOND`       | Full operating-envelope claim, measured plant and timing bounds, independently validated permission and fallback | Policy proposes across full *signed* task envelope; every action passes the enforcer                                      | Evidence, configuration, calibration, or standing premise fails |
| `COND`         | Restricted operating-envelope claim and its own evidence, limits, and fault coverage                             | Policy proposes only within signed reduced limits; every action passes the enforcer                                       | Any restricted premise becomes false or unknown                 |
| `REFUSE`       | Missing, contradictory, expired, or unauthenticated critical evidence                                            | No operating permit; execute the assessed stop or hold, the fallback-ladder rung the release case validates for the plant | Re-adjudication with repaired evidence                          |

: **Three signed release verdicts for the mobile manipulator**: Full operation and restricted mode both retain independent per-action permission. Refusal is an actionable engineering result. {#tbl-16-verdicts-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[14,32,32,22]"}

Each verdict in @tbl-16-verdicts-taxonomy is signed against the physical state of the machine at the moment of evaluation. The right-hand column of the table therefore pairs every operational grant with an explicit expiry or refusal trigger, because a brake lining or sensor mount that passed inspection before commissioning does not stay in its commissioning state. As the physical plant wears and drifts over time, a release verdict holds only while runtime checks, scheduled measurements, and enforced site procedures continue to verify its standing premises.

## The Verdict's Standing Conditions {#sec-release-standing-conditions}

A signed release can lapse without any change to the underlying software. Brake linings wear down, camera brackets shift under continuous vibration, or warehouse traffic polishes concrete lanes until traction drops. When these physical premises drift, the stopping claim certified by the adjudicator no longer holds. Standing conditions bind the operational verdict to these physical baselines by defining an explicit observation cadence for each premise alongside deterministic fallback responses when a check fails. Because failure modes originate in hardware and environment, their observation schedules must follow physical degradation mechanisms rather than software sprint schedules. An assurance case maintained this way, its validity updated throughout operating life as monitored evidence shifts, is what the safety literature calls a *dynamic safety case*\index{Safety case!dynamic} [@denney2015dynamic].

### Degradation, drift, and observation cadence {#sec-release-calibration-drift}

None of the three verdicts is a permanent grant. Mechanical linkages develop backlash, friction surfaces wear, optical lenses collect dust, and operating environments change. Operating under either an unconditional (`UNCOND`) or conditional (`COND`) verdict therefore carries continuous obligations for the life of the deployment. Notebook \ref{nbk-release-aisle-spare} shows how little wear the stopping claim tolerates. A credible deceleration `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_shortfall_pct_str` below the assumed `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` spends the whole partial spare, and a smaller loss spends the reserve that remains once admission work is charged, leaving no allowance for perception latency or traction variation. A lining that wears that far is discovered at a rack end as an overrun unless the degradation first trips a standing condition, such as a scheduled loaded deceleration trial or an automated pre-shift brake diagnostic, before the machine is cleared to enter the aisle. Every operational obligation pairs a physical premise with an automated detector and an immediate mitigation, establishing a standing condition tied to the release verdict.

Sensor mounting drift can silently invalidate localization while every camera frame stays sharp and fresh. Daily thermal cycling and machine vibration alter extrinsic sensor geometry, and software rollback cannot realign a physically displaced bracket. The safety case must therefore require qualified online drift detection or scheduled physical recalibrations, setting inspection intervals from the underlying mechanical wear rates. A cryptographic checksum confirms only that the stored calibration file matches its build artifact; it gives no evidence that the physical camera still sits at that modeled pose.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-standing-premises
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STANDING PREMISES OF THE MACHINE'S RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-standing-conditions (opening paragraph and the
# │          envelope-membership paragraph).
# │ Goal: Tie the standing conditions to the premises the machine's claims use.
# │ Show: friction needed for a_brake against dry concrete, tote-rack capacity,
# │       and the base tracking bound.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; mu_min = a_brake / g (calc_required_friction) assumes
# │      all weight on driven wheels (optimistic screening). The permission
# │      rail's hold-up is sized in @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder; the
# │      manifest only signs it.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_mass, fmt_length, check
from mlsysim.physics.drivetrain import calc_required_friction

class ReleaseStandingPremises:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
    AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    mu_min = calc_required_friction(AISLE.a_brake)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction floor 0.204")
    check(mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Dry concrete exceeds the friction floor")
    check(abs(RM.onboard_payload_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity 50 kg")
    check(abs(AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Tracking bound 40 mm")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(RM.onboard_payload_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    eps_track_str = fmt_length(AISLE.eps_track, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

A release verdict depends on physical premises with widely differing observation schedules. For instance, the mobile manipulator's optimistic all-weight traction screen requires a floor friction coefficient of at least `{python} ReleaseStandingPremises.mu_min_str`; the braking claim additionally requires qualified loaded wheel forces, drive conditions, and stopping traces. Dry concrete exceeds this threshold by a wide margin, at roughly `{python} ReleaseStandingPremises.mu_dry_str`, but a baseline site survey conducted before commissioning cannot guarantee surface conditions against fluid spills or traffic polishing over time. The safety case must therefore specify routine floor maintenance schedules alongside strict exclusion rules whenever surface contamination occurs, supplemented by any onboard traction monitoring. Similarly, the arm's contact-force sensors require periodic recalibration against reference loads. Every physical premise must be rechecked continuously or periodically at a cadence matched to how fast it degrades. This is the fourth law, *permission must be earned* (principle \ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority}), applied over time. The verdict grants permission contingent on operating conditions, and that permission endures only while the evidence supporting each premise remains valid.

Every runtime-monitored premise requires a dedicated detector and a pre-allocated fallback response; conversely, premises governed by facility maintenance require accountable operators and enforceable exclusion rules. If a safety case credits a navigation-camera dispatch age of `{python} ReleaseClaims.t_age_str`, the runtime monitor must measure frame arrival latency against hardware clocks, accounting for sensor readout and transport delays separately. Forwarding an unverified metadata timestamp does not confirm that the frame is fresh. Without hardware-synchronized event timestamps, unverified inputs quietly turn safety premises into ungrounded assumptions. Different premises demand different sampling frequencies. The tote-rack load, bounded by its `{python} ReleaseStandingPremises.payload_str` mechanical payload limit, can be checked at each load-changing event if access controls exclude unrecorded loading and the check completes before the changed load receives motion authority. Conversely, base velocity, position tracking, and action lease validity must be evaluated deterministically on every `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_tick_str` safety-enforcer tick.

### The envelope trichotomy and epistemic gaps {#sec-release-envelope-trichotomy-sub}

A naive binary health check assumes normal operation whenever no explicit error flag is asserted, mistaking a dead sensor or a diverged filter for safe clearance. Checking monitored premises at runtime instead exposes three states of **envelope membership**\index{Envelope membership!trichotomy states}: known-true, known-false, and unknown. Membership is *known-true* when authenticated telemetry and hardware-referenced timestamps confirm that the plant's bounded state-uncertainty set remains strictly inside certified envelope boundaries. Estimator convergence or small covariance matrices alone do not prove containment if model assumptions have broken down. When measured telemetry reveals a physical boundary violation, such as base tracking error exceeding the `{python} ReleaseStandingPremises.eps_track_str` bound reserved within the stopping envelope, the state is *known-false*. Finally, when an optical encoder loses serial communication, a camera frame fails its cyclic redundancy check (CRC), or an extended Kalman filter diverges, the system enters an *epistemic gap*. In this *unknown* state, the controller cannot tell whether the physical machine is safely positioned or breaching clearance margins.

When telemetry supporting active motion becomes unknown or known-false, the safety enforcer revokes trajectory tracking and executes the pre-certified fallback procedure for the plant's dynamic state. This runtime intervention differs from rejecting an invalid future trajectory proposal, because an already active trajectory chunk can continue executing only while its supporting sensor evidence, physical bounds, and lease duration remain intact. The system's flight recorder must log whether revocation stemmed from unobservable state telemetry or an active boundary breach, while the hardware supplies enough reserve energy and sensing capability to bring the plant to a controlled stop or hold.

::: {#dfn-release-envelope-trichotomy .callout-definition title="Envelope trichotomy"}

![](images/svg/dfn_envelope_trichotomy.svg){fig-alt="Three boxes left to right: known-true with a qualified uncertainty set inside the envelope and fresh verified evidence; unknown, reached when evidence is lost, from dropout, CRC mismatch, or estimator divergence; and known-false, reached over the top when a boundary breach is measured, such as tracking error above its bound. A bracket under known-true reads permit equals 1, tracking may continue. One bracket under unknown and known-false reads permit equals 0, validated stop or hold, logged causes stay distinct." width=100%}

***Envelope trichotomy***\index{Envelope trichotomy!definition}\index{Operating envelope!trichotomy} is the three-state epistemic classification of cyber-physical system health relative to its signed operating envelope: *known-true* (qualified state-uncertainty set contained inside the supported envelope), *known-false* (verified boundary violation triggering deterministic hardware refusal), and *unknown* (state uncertainty caused by sensor dropout, frame corruption, or estimator divergence).

1.  **Significance**: An unknown state is not evidence of a boundary breach, yet neither condition permits continued tracking. The permission decision is refusal in both unknown and known-false states; the logged cause remains distinct and the response depends on the plant's validated stop or hold capability.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a binary boolean status check (`is_safe == true`), the envelope trichotomy separates sensor blindness from active violations, ensuring telemetry loss is never mistaken for safe clearance.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating a stored command as indefinitely valid after communication fails. An active chunk may continue only within its own still-valid evidence and lease; otherwise the assessed fallback must take over.

:::

The same three-state distinction applies to verification test records. A test trial marked `UNOBSERVABLE` or `INVALID` during acceptance testing (@sec-verification-four-verdicts) cannot establish the claim its required witnesses or test conditions failed to resolve. It leaves a gap in that coverage; other valid records remain evidence only for the conditions and claims they establish. Verified `PASS` records support the claims covered by their conditions and witnesses. A valid `FAIL` contradicts the claim tested under those conditions and withdraws any authorization that relies on it.

### Blind travel, kinetic consequences, and cycle limits {#sec-release-blind-travel-limits}

When telemetry fails or sensors black out, a machine traveling without sensory feedback moves blind; it must execute a deterministic fallback stop before its forward travel consumes the remaining spatial clearance. How fast that clearance vanishes depends directly on vehicle speed, contact geometry, and available actuator authority. Sizing the response therefore requires calculating the kinetic energy and blind travel accumulated during each millisecond of delay, and matching each sensor loss to a pre-certified fallback path.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-blind-travel
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BLIND TRAVEL AND THE FALLBACK RESPONSE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-standing-conditions (fallback-response paragraph and
# │          the enforcement-path paragraph after it).
# │ Goal: Size the consequence of continuing without telemetry on the machine.
# │ Show: loaded kinetic energy at aisle speed, travel per millisecond, the
# │       degraded-mode speed, the permission tick, renewal-to-onset time, and
# │       the response to a premise the enforcer monitors itself.
# │ How: calc_kinetic_energy with RM.loaded_mass and AISLE.v_aisle; the two
# │      routes to brake onset are the renewal- and flag-referenced stops
# │      (Scenarios.WarehouseRenewalReferencedStop, ...FlagReferencedStop).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_energy, fmt_mass, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_kinetic_energy

class ReleaseBlindTravel:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine, plus one chapter-local input ────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
    AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
    degraded_fraction = 0.5  # category: chosen (degraded mode halves the aisle speed)
    SILENT = Scenarios.WarehouseRenewalReferencedStop  # category: illustrative (onset bound after the last valid renewal)
    FLAGGED = Scenarios.WarehouseFlagReferencedStop  # category: illustrative (onset bound after a monitored premise's flag)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    e_k_loaded = calc_kinetic_energy(RM.loaded_mass, AISLE.v_aisle).to(joule)
    travel_per_ms = SILENT.result.travel_over(1 * millisecond).to(millimeter)
    v_degraded = (degraded_fraction * AISLE.v_aisle).to(meter / second)
    t_renewal_to_onset = SILENT.delay.to(millisecond)
    t_monitor_response = FLAGGED.delay.to(millisecond)  # enforcer-detected premise
    # Notebook (nbk-release-silent-proposer-window): travel to brake onset on each
    # route, and the flag latency at which the monitored route stops no sooner.
    d_silent = SILENT.result.delay_travel.to(millimeter)
    d_monitored = FLAGGED.result.delay_travel.to(millimeter)
    t_flag_crossover = (t_renewal_to_onset - t_monitor_response).to(millisecond)
    d_saved = (d_silent - d_monitored).to(millimeter)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond)
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond)
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus.to(millisecond)
    t_onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond)
    t_silent = t_renewal_to_onset
    t_monitored = t_monitor_response

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(e_k_loaded.magnitude - 310.96) < 0.01, "Loaded kinetic energy at 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(travel_per_ms.magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "1.3 mm of travel per millisecond")
    check(abs(v_degraded.magnitude - 0.65) < 1e-9, "Degraded mode at 0.65 m/s")
    check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Renewal to brake onset 82 ms")
    check(abs(t_monitor_response.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "Enforcer tick + bus + brake onset 22 ms")
    # margin_silent_proposer_response_strip.svg fig-alt hand-types the lease and each window
    check(abs(AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk lease 60 ms")
    check(abs(AISLE.t_bus.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Bus transfer 1 ms")
    check(abs(AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, "Brake onset 20 ms")
    check(abs(d_silent.magnitude - 106.6) < 1e-9, "Silent proposer: 106.6 mm to brake onset")
    check(abs(d_monitored.magnitude - 28.6) < 1e-9, "Monitored premise, immediate flag: 28.6 mm")
    check(abs(t_flag_crossover.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Flag-latency crossover equals the 60 ms lease")
    check(abs(d_saved.magnitude - 78.0) < 1e-9, "Monitoring saves at most 78.0 mm")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    e_k_str = fmt_energy(round(e_k_loaded.magnitude) * joule, unit=joule, precision=0)
    travel_per_ms_str = fmt_length(travel_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_degraded_str = fmt_velocity(v_degraded, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_monitor_response_str = fmt_latency(t_monitor_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_onset_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_brake_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_silent_str = fmt_length(d_silent, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_monitored_str = fmt_length(d_monitored, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_flag_crossover_str = fmt_latency(t_flag_crossover, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_saved_str = fmt_length(d_saved, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

How the system responds when a premise cannot be checked must follow from the physics of unmonitored motion rather than from arbitrary severity categories. When the mobile manipulator traverses an aisle at `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.v_aisle_str` with its tote rack fully loaded, its `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.m1_str` mass carries `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.e_k_str` of kinetic energy. If its primary lidar stops updating, every millisecond of blind travel carries the base `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.travel_per_ms_str` closer to potential obstacles. The safety case pre-certifies three possible fallback paths, two of which apply only when the signed release names them in advance. The first is a degraded mode\index{Degraded mode!velocity reduction} that permits continued motion while diverse redundant sensors keep state uncertainty bounded, for example throttling the aisle speed to `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.v_degraded_str` (half the aisle speed, a chosen value) while secondary sensors watch the path. The second is a switch to a restricted limit set that a signed `COND` case\index{Release verdict!conditional} pre-validated for that exact sensor loss, if the release includes one. The runtime only selects that profile; it does not create a new verdict. Dead reckoning and wheel odometry may retain qualified position bounds over a brief window, but cannot verify obstacle clearance on their own. The third option, the hardware STOP response\index{Fallback ladder!STOP rung}, handles complete loss of observability by executing a configured drive and brake sequence. Stopping the vehicle within available clearance margins requires calibrated response timing, sufficient drive traction, and known brake deceleration.

Action leases bound how long an admitted trajectory chunk may run without renewal. Checking this lease on every controller tick does not require re-measuring every long-term site condition. Instead, the runtime permission path checks fresh local sensor telemetry alongside the signed validity windows of slower site inspections and maintenance records. If the proposer stalls or its communication drops, task throughput suffers, but safety holds as long as the enforcer and its fallback path remain decoupled, responsive, and intact.

Any standing condition governing physical motion requires an enforcement path with a measured detection and response budget. In this book's architecture, an independent safety enforcer\index{Safety enforcer!hardware interlock} checks trajectory proposals and monitored premises before issuing actuator permissions, re-evaluating system state on every `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_tick_str` control tick. A subsystem failure reaches this enforcer along one of two paths: a silent proposer that stops transmitting is caught only when its existing action lease expires, whereas an actively monitored hardware fault raises an immediate interrupt flag. Because detection delays differ between these paths, so does the distance the base travels blind (notebook \ref{nbk-release-silent-proposer-window}).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_silent_proposer_response_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal timelines in milliseconds. Silent proposer: a 60-millisecond lease, 2 milliseconds of tick and bus transfer, and 20 milliseconds of brake onset, 82 milliseconds in total. Monitored premise: the same 2 milliseconds and 20 milliseconds, 22 milliseconds in total."}

*The lease dominates: a silent proposer reaches brake onset in `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_renewal_to_onset_str`, a flagged premise in `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_monitor_response_str`.*
:::

::: {#nbk-release-silent-proposer-window .callout-notebook title="The silent-proposer window"}

**Problem**: The base runs the aisle at `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.v_aisle_str`. How far does it travel before brake onset when the proposer falls silent, how far when a monitored premise fails and its flag reaches the enforcer at once, and how late may that flag arrive before monitoring stops the base no sooner than the lease would?

**Variables**:

- Aisle speed $\SpeedAtDetection =$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.v_aisle_str` (Chosen), so `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.travel_per_ms_str` of travel per millisecond
- Chunk lease `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_lease_str` and permission tick `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_tick_str` (Chosen); bus transfer `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_bus_str` and brake onset `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_onset_str` (Illustrative)
- Flag latency $\FailureFlagLatency$ from the physical failure to a flag the enforcer can read (Unknown; the detector's qualification must bound it)

**Math**:

1. **Silent proposer**: `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_lease_str` $+$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_tick_str` $+$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_bus_str` $+$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_onset_str` $=$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_renewal_to_onset_str`, and `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.v_aisle_str` $\times$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_renewal_to_onset_str` $=$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.d_silent_str`.
2. **Monitored premise, immediate flag**: `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_tick_str` $+$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_bus_str` $+$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_onset_str` $=$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_monitor_response_str`, and `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.v_aisle_str` $\times$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_monitor_response_str` $=$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.d_monitored_str`.
3. **Crossover**: $\FailureFlagLatency +$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_monitor_response_str` $=$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_renewal_to_onset_str` at $\FailureFlagLatency =$ `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_flag_crossover_str`, the length of the lease itself.

**Result**: Monitoring can save up to `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.d_saved_str` of travel, but only for a flag that arrives within `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_flag_crossover_str` of the failure; a slower flag stops the base no sooner than waiting out the lease.

**Systems insight**: The `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_monitor_response_str` local subtotal is not a complete detection-to-stop time; it reflects only controller cycle delay, communication transfer, and physical brake engagement. The decisive term governing whether an active monitor preserves physical clearance is $\FailureFlagLatency$, the hardware detection latency. If an architectural budget fails to bound $\FailureFlagLatency$, the safety case cannot claim proactive protection. Every millisecond spent detecting a fault carries the loaded vehicle another `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.travel_per_ms_str` toward whatever the failed premise was protecting against.

:::

When an operating premise transitions to unknown or known-false, the enforcer revokes trajectory tracking and commands the appropriate rung of the fallback ladder, and the signed safety case must specify both this fallback selection and its measured timing. For the mobile base, the certified stopping sequence uses controlled, powered deceleration to bring the wheels to rest before applying electromechanical holding brakes. Because digital controller logic and brake-coil hold-up capacitors cannot deliver drive motor torque, the safety case must confirm drive energy, feedback sensing, and inverter continuity across every fault condition expected to use this active deceleration profile. By contrast, a raw torque-inhibit or free-wheeling cutoff is a different physical response; it cannot inherit stopping-distance guarantees calculated for controlled electrical braking.

Entering an unknown or known-false state also triggers local black-box logging. The onboard recorder must preserve the telemetry window leading up to refusal alongside the execution of the fallback trajectory, even if the initiating fault cuts external networking or primary bus power. These records are essential for root-cause investigation, but writing them to nonvolatile storage must never delay the hard real-time safety stop; @sec-release-data-curation-flywheel sizes the capture path.

On longer timescales, even when every runtime heartbeat succeeds, the **release verdict**\index{Release verdict!invalidation} carries an operational cycle and inspection budget.[^fn-rule-fatigue-derating] Operating hours and mechanical fatigue wear components in ways that high-frequency telemetry cannot observe directly (such as surface pitting on gear teeth, elastomer seal stiffening, or fastener preload relaxation). Once this cycle budget expires, the release case must be re-adjudicated before autonomous motion can resume. Across every timescale, a deployment verdict remains valid only while its supporting standing conditions remain demonstrably known-true, checked at intervals matched to physical wear rates and backed by pre-certified fallback stops with measured latencies. Claims, verdicts, and revocation conditions are now defined. The six claims of the warehouse mobile manipulator can be adjudicated against the physical evidence assembled across this book.

[^fn-rule-fatigue-derating]: **Mechanical Fatigue Budget**\index{Fatigue limits!cyclic derating}: A cumulative-damage model such as Miner's rule ($\sum_i \AppliedLoadCycleCount_i/\FatigueLifeCycleCount_i$) [@miner1945cumulative] can organize a measured load spectrum against component-specific fatigue data; it is an approximation, not a universal failure deadline. The assessed loads, uncertainty, inspection evidence, and stopping consequences determine any signed payload derating and cycle limit. An expired limit revokes the applicable release case rather than silently extending service.

## Adjudicating the Safety Case {#sec-release-case-worked-full}

An algebraically exact stopping equation or contact-force bound still fails to protect a machine if the physical premise beneath its warrant has never been measured on hardware. Adjudicating a safety release case requires checking each warrant against the qualified measurements, justified analysis, or validated operating restrictions that support it. For the warehouse mobile manipulator, the adjudicator takes each of the six claims of @tbl-16-cae-scorecard in turn, names the physical premise under its warrant, and grades the evidence behind that premise. This isolates the exact boundary where mathematical deduction ends and physical measurement must take over.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-worked-verdict
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ADJUDICATING THE MACHINE'S RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-case-worked-full (the door branch cites
# │          @eq-release-trip-indentation and @eq-release-coupled-indentation,
# │          derived in @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact), and
# │          @tbl-16-cond-measurements.
# │ Goal: Show that each claim's warrant rests on a premise the book's evidence
# │       leaves illustrative, and list the measurements that would move it.
# │ Show: latch force at brake command and the arm stop it requires at the
# │       guarded and unsupported approaches; the base budget and spare; the
# │       illustrative value behind each premise; the handover force; the
# │       restricted aisle speed a COND case could sign.
# │ How: latch and handover premises from EnforcementContactForce
# │      (calc-release-contact-premises); the budget and ceilings from the
# │      finished budgets (Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed,
# │      ...InspectedFloor, ...WithDispatch; jerk-limited S-curve stop, jerk
# │      bound = the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit).
# │ Note:    Reads v_restricted from ReleaseEnvelope (calc-release-operating-
# │          envelope), so the chosen restricted speed is set in one place.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_force, fmt_sci_qty, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
from mlsysim.physics.drivetrain import calc_required_friction

class ReleaseWorkedVerdict:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
```
