```{python}
    AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
    g_std = (1 * standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)
    g = g_std
    v_latch = AISLE.v_latch_approach
    v_latch_high = AISLE.v_latch_high
    v_restricted = ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted  # chosen; set once in calc-release-operating-envelope
    STOP = Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopAtAisleSpeed  # category: illustrative (finished budget at the aisle speed)
    INSPECTED = Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopInspectedFloor  # category: illustrative (same budget, inspected-floor traction)
    DISPATCH = Scenarios.WarehouseFinishedStopWithDispatch  # category: illustrative (same budget, Delta_da charged)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE: the door branch, then the base spare ──────────────────────────
    # Door branch: premises from the enforcement record (calc-release-contact-premises).
    f_cmd_lo = EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd
    x_rem_lo = EnforcementContactForce.x_rem
    a_arm_lo = EnforcementContactForce.a_arm
    t_arm_stop = EnforcementContactForce.t_arm_stop
    f_cmd_hi = EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd_hi
    a_arm_hi = EnforcementContactForce.a_arm_hi

    # Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
    j_brake = STOP.jerk.to(meter / second**3)
    budget_aisle = STOP.result.required_distance.to(millimeter)
    spare_aisle = STOP.result.spare.to(millimeter)
    mu_min = calc_required_friction(AISLE.a_brake)
    # Optimistic all-weight-on-driven-wheels traction screen; actual loaded stopping needs qualification.
    # The jerk bound belongs to the load and is unchanged.
    a_inspected = INSPECTED.deceleration.to(meter / second**2)
    v_inspected_ceiling = INSPECTED.result.speed_ceiling.to(meter / second)
    v_ceiling = STOP.result.speed_ceiling.to(meter / second)
    t_renewal_to_onset = Scenarios.WarehouseRenewalReferencedStop.delay.to(millisecond)
    f_handover = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover
    # Checkpoint estimate (chk-release-refusal-and-path-to-cond): a loaded trial whose
    # low tail falls short of a_brake. The answer is not printed; the guard keeps the
    # item's premise (the reserve after Delta_da turns negative) true.
    a_trial = 1.6 * meter / second**2  # category: illustrative (hypothetical low-tail loaded deceleration)
    reserve_trial = DISPATCH.variant(deceleration=a_trial).result.spare.to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose and the table ──────────────────
    check(abs(f_cmd_lo.magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake command, guarded approach")
    check(abs(x_rem_lo.magnitude - 0.1525) < 1e-6, "Remaining compression 0.15 mm")
    check(abs(a_arm_lo.magnitude - 2.95) < 0.005, "Arm stop premise about 3 m/s^2 (computed 2.95)")
    check(abs(t_arm_stop.magnitude - 10.0) < 0.5, "Arm stop takes about 10 ms")
    check(abs(f_cmd_hi.magnitude - 95.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake command, unsupported approach")
    check(abs(a_arm_hi.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-6, "Unsupported approach needs 400 m/s^2")
    check(abs(spare_aisle.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction floor 0.204")
    check(abs(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, "Inspected-floor ceiling 1.23 m/s")
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, "Aisle ceiling 1.44 m/s")
    check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Renewal to brake onset 82 ms")
    check(RM.chunk_inference_latency < AISLE.t_lease, "Chunk inference fits inside the lease")
    check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "Transient handover force 20.7 N")
    check(v_restricted < v_inspected_ceiling < AISLE.v_aisle, "Restricted mode sits below the inspected-floor ceiling")
    a_arm_ratio = (a_arm_hi / a_arm_lo).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    # margin_arm_stop_demand_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 3, 9.8 and 400 m/s^2; caption says over a hundredfold
    check(abs(a_arm_ratio - 135.6) < 0.1, "The unsupported approach needs about 136 times the guarded arm stop")
    check(abs(g_std.magnitude - 9.80665) < 1e-9, "Standard gravity 9.8 m/s^2")
    check(AISLE.v_aisle >= a_trial**2 / j_brake, "Checkpoint trial stop stays in the trapezoidal regime")
    check(reserve_trial.magnitude < 0 < spare_aisle.magnitude, "Checkpoint: a 1.6 m/s^2 low tail leaves no reserve once Delta_da is charged")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Door branch of C1
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    k_latch_str = fmt_sci_qty(AISLE.k_latch, newton / meter, precision=1)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_cmd_str = fmt_force(f_cmd_lo, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_rem_lo.magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm_lo.magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    t_arm_stop_str = fmt_latency(round(t_arm_stop.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_high, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_cmd_high_str = fmt_force(f_cmd_hi, precision=0)
    a_arm_high_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm_hi, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    # Other branches
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    enforcer_unloaded_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_unloaded, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.perception_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    # Measurement table: the illustrative value behind each premise
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_brake_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    eps_track_str = fmt_length(AISLE.eps_track, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(AISLE.delta_loc, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    v_inspected_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(RM.chunk_inference_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_handover, precision=1)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_arm_ratio_str = fmt_int(round(a_arm_ratio))
    a_trial_str = fmt_acceleration(a_trial, unit=meter / second**2, precision=1)
```

The door-opening branch of C1 shows the procedure in full. The contact enforcement record supplies the branch's underlying mechanics (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact). At the guarded approach velocity of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_latch_str`, @eq-release-trip-indentation yields an impact force at physical braking onset of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.f_cmd_str`, well below the `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.f_latch_limit_str` latch limit. From there, @eq-release-coupled-indentation leaves the latch plate with only `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.x_remaining_str` of additional allowable compression. Bringing the arm to rest within this narrow mechanical travel requires a deceleration of approximately `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_str` over a brief `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_arm_stop_str` stopping window. By contrast, at the unconstrained approach velocity of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_latch_high_str`, the force at braking onset rises to `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.f_cmd_high_str`, and avoiding structural damage demands a deceleration of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_high_str`, more than an order of magnitude above standard gravity. While this kinematic calculation specifies the stopping performance required for release, mathematical derivation alone cannot prove that the physical arm actuators can deliver it. Consequently, the operating envelope (@tbl-16-odd-invariants) excludes the high-speed approach. Raising approach speeds sharply escalates contact braking demands, whereas the system's training demonstrations offer zero empirical evidence for safe high-speed contact (@sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability-geometry).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_arm_stop_demand_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Log-scale ladder of three horizontal bars for the arm deceleration needed to stop inside the latch: 400 meters per second squared at a 0.10 meters per second approach, a gray reference bar for 1 g at 9.8, and 3 meters per second squared at the guarded 0.03 meters per second approach."}

*Raising the approach from `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_latch_str` to `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_latch_high_str` multiplies the arm stop needed `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_ratio_str`-fold.*
:::

Neither result is in doubt as arithmetic; the algebraic deduction is exact. Formal engineering release, however, cannot rest on closed-form kinematic models alone. The door branch fails authorization because its safety warrant depends on an unverified physical premise. Whether the physical manipulator, carrying its link momentum, payload mass, and reflected rotor inertia, can actually deliver `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_str` of deceleration within a fraction of a millimeter depends on transient joint torque limits, motor electrical time constants, and structural stiffness. Without calibrated hardware traces measuring these dynamic properties under load, this mechanical premise remains *unknown*, and the adjudicator must refuse the claim.

The remaining claim branches fail on similar grounds:

- **Base braking corridor (C1)**: The base stopping budget of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.budget_str` omits dispatch-to-admission delay and rests on illustrative values for braking deceleration, brake onset, path-tracking error, and localization uncertainty. Its remaining margin of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.spare_str` can be exhausted by the illustrative deceleration shortfall in step 4 of notebook \ref{nbk-release-aisle-spare}, and step 5 leaves still less once admission work is charged.
- **Object handover (C1)**: The mug handover branch fails on three separate premises. First, the calculated contact force falls below the criterion only for an unconstrained, free-moving hand, and it comes from a standardized biomechanical body model rather than a force measurement of this contact. Second, the evidence packet does not show that the coworker's hand cannot be trapped against a rigid fixture, so the non-clamping geometry is unproven. Third, perceptual grounding remains unverified: a proposal that mistakes a clear glass jar for the target mug satisfies every geometric affordance check, and no trace in the runtime logs disambiguates the object.
- **Enforcer timing (C2)**: The timing warrant for the runtime safety enforcer assumes a worst-case execution time (WCET) of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.wcet_str` against an unloaded baseline of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.enforcer_unloaded_str` and a `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.deadline_str` deadline. The WCET is declared without architectural analysis and loaded stress evidence supporting it under peak memory bus saturation.
- **Traction and environmental state (C3)**: Claim C3 requires a qualified friction floor across every authorized aisle; `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.mu_min_str` is only the optimistic all-weight traction screen, not a sufficient loaded stopping qualification. A clean concrete floor can be validated through baseline skid testing, but the onboard cameras cannot reliably distinguish dry concrete from a thin film of transparent oil, and no sensor on the machine can exclude liquid contamination ahead of the braking contact.
- **Perception pipeline latency (C4)**: The `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_age_str` dispatch age combines nominal datasheet readout times with uncharacterized pipeline delays rather than verified end-to-end telemetry.
- **Permission independence (C5)**: The placement record's loaded test report, which would show the enforcer's maxima under the proposer's worst interference and test the common causes of @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die, is described in this book but not produced. Without it, the credited enforcement isolation is unsubstantiated; even supporting isolation records would not by themselves establish statistical independence of every failure event.
- **Authority transfer (C6)**: The argument cites `PASS` fault records for authority transitions A1 through A4, and no such records exist yet. Local operation could drop the remote-channel cases, but not the local ones.

Because every claim rests on at least one unverified physical premise, the adjudicator must render a verdict of `REFUSE`. This refusal does not imply that the robot is inherently dangerous. The book's supporting inputs are illustrative models rather than empirical validation logs, so the verdict is illustrative as well; it models how release is adjudicated and shows why ungrounded claims cannot license physical deployment. The fourth law, *permission must be earned*, requires an operational restriction wherever the available evidence cannot support a premise. Here, every branch contains an unverified premise. A principled refusal must therefore specify the exact measurements required to turn an unverified assumption into an accepted warrant. @Tbl-16-cond-measurements lists these evidentiary requirements, naming the physical premise each measurement settles and the operational restriction a supporting result would lift.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The four bedrock laws, the fourth of which holds that permission must be earned, are established in @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws.
:::

| Measurement                           | Premise it settles (value in this book)                                                                                                            | Claims | What a supporting result lifts                                                                                                                                                                |
|:--------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Stopping trials at the loaded mass    | Low-tail credible deceleration (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_brake_str`)                                                                       | C1     | The base's budget and its `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_ceiling_str` ceiling, so an aisle speed can be signed                                                                              |
| Brake-onset trials                    | Brake onset (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_act_str`)                                                                                            | C1, C2 | The `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_renewal_to_onset_str` bound from the last valid renewal to brake onset                                                                                   |
| End-to-end age trace                  | Dispatch age (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_age_str`) and subsequent evidence aging                                                             | C4     | The age term of the budget and the stale-data threshold                                                                                                                                       |
| Tracking-error and localization tails | Tracking bound (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.eps_track_str`) and localization bound (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.delta_loc_str`)              | C1     | The inset and overhead terms of the budget                                                                                                                                                    |
| Site survey                           | Rack-end clear distance (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.d_clear_str`)                                                                              | C1     | A signed speed at each surveyed rack end                                                                                                                                                      |
| Floor survey                          | Dry-floor friction (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.mu_dry_str`) against the `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.mu_min_str` needed                      | C3     | Assessed route only, with maintained contamination exclusion and loaded stops at the qualified friction floor; reduced speed alone cannot exclude oil                                         |
| Inference trace                       | Chunk inference at the 99th percentile (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_chunk_str`)                                                               | None   | Service availability: characterize renewal within the `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_lease_str` lease; a percentile does not guarantee each renewal, and C2 depends on independent fallback |
| Loaded enforcer timing                | Enforcer WCET (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.wcet_str`, declared)                                                                                 | C2, C5 | The `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.deadline_str` deadline under the placement's worst load                                                                                                    |
| Arm stopping trials                   | Arm deceleration from the guarded approach (about `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_str` needed)                                                | C1     | Door opening at the guarded approach                                                                                                                                                          |
| Handover force trials                 | Peak contact force at the handover speed (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.f_handover_str` derived for a free hand) and absence of clamping geometry | C1     | Handing the mug to the coworker at `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_handover_str` under `accept_item`                                                                                         |
| Operator trials                       | Takeover and authority-handover timing                                                                                                             | C6     | Remote takeover, once A1–A4 each have a `PASS` record; otherwise local operation only                                                                                                         |

: **Measurements that would move the verdict toward `COND`**: Each row names the premise a measurement settles on the warehouse mobile manipulator and the restriction a supporting result would lift; the inference trace bears on service availability only. {#tbl-16-cond-measurements tbl-colwidths="[20,30,8,42]"}

Neural network inference latency primarily governs system availability rather than baseline safety. An inference overrun will not violate physical containment so long as the independent hardware safety path and powered fallback controllers remain operational; however, repeated deadline misses will degrade throughput and stall task progress. Conversely, resource contention across shared memory, PCIe buses, or CPU caches that delays the runtime enforcer or starves its sensor feeds represents a direct safety failure under claims C2 and C5. Finally, while local autonomous operation can safely omit validation trials for unused remote teleoperation links, deployment still requires verified software placement records, comprehensive common-cause fault coverage, and passing test records for every local authority transition.

### Worked restricted service with stipulated evidence {#sec-release-stipulated-service}

Without calibrated hardware measurements, the mobile manipulator remains locked out under a `REFUSE` verdict. To see how an engineering organization moves from initial refusal to conditional deployment without relaxing its structural safety limits, consider a **stipulated** release case in which an engineering packet supplies the measured traces specified below. (The uncalibrated evidence currently available in this book continues to dictate `REFUSE`.)

The target application is *restricted inspected-route mug delivery*. The robot retrieves a declared mug from a singulated feeder and traverses a designated, surveyed warehouse aisle at a velocity capped at `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_restricted_str`. It then pauses the mobile base to open an equipment cage latch using the guarded contact trajectory and hands the mug to a consenting human coworker under the `accept_item` primitive at `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_handover_str`. Operational authority remains strictly local. The feeder mechanism physically prevents accidental object substitutions, recognizing that singulation alone cannot authenticate identity. Similarly, strict access controls prevent personnel from stepping into the robot's active stopping corridor during transit.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The difference between a coworker who consents to a machine's risk, as this one does, and people who bear it without choosing, is developed in @sec-responsibility-who-bears-risk.
:::

For claim C1, the safety case stipulates empirical stopping traces under full payload mass, measured tracking and localization variance, dynamic latch-stopping performance, and instrumented handover contact forces that satisfy the bounded thresholds in @tbl-16-cond-measurements. For claims C2 and C5, the case stipulates independent hardware fault-injection logs and worst-case execution timing traces gathered under peak synthetic computational load. These records must account for common-cause hardware failures, support the enforcer's permission deadlines and actuator reaction latencies, separate controlled motor deceleration from passive mechanical braking at rest, and confirm isolated drive-energy cutoff and sensor integrity under all credited fault modes.

For claim C4, the case stipulates synchronized end-to-end hardware timestamp telemetry, bounded clock skew, and a verified upper bound on dispatch-to-admission latency. This latency must be deducted from the dynamic stopping distance budget so that a strictly positive safety margin remains; a theoretical kinematic velocity ceiling cannot authorize transit speeds on its own. Because sensor data ages continuously throughout execution, the chunk lease starts only when a plan is admitted, never when it is computed. The qualification packet must also check the time between admitted plans against the lease renewal deadline rather than assuming that nominal policy inference frequency guarantees admission. For claim C6, the packet stipulates verified `PASS` audit records across every state transition exercised by the local autonomous executive, while disabling the unverified remote teleoperation interface entirely.

Claim C3 requires substantially more than visual inspection or reduced transit velocity. The case stipulates a qualified site friction survey showing a friction coefficient of at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str` across the surveyed transit corridor, reinforced by active cleaning protocols, chemical containment barriers, and physical access gates that maintain floor integrity throughout the authorized inspection interval. Stopping trials at maximum payload must confirm deceleration on this specific friction surface with the loaded wheel distribution and drive settings of the signed configuration. The complete restricted stopping distance, including the verified dispatch-to-admission delay bound and a positive safety margin, must fit inside the surveyed physical clearance with a positive reserve, the same accounting as step 5 of notebook \ref{nbk-release-aisle-spare}. The operating velocity of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_restricted_str` sits below the partial ceiling of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_inspected_ceiling_str`, but that comparison is only an initial feasibility filter. The active transit permit is revoked immediately upon any reported spill, expired maintenance inspection, or perimeter breach. If unmonitored oil or other fluid can enter the corridor during the deployment window, the stipulation is invalidated and the verdict reverts to `REFUSE`. A lower speed cannot repair that premise, because the restricted speed was sized for the inspected friction floor of `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`, not for a film near `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str` that removes most of it.

The task capability packet is similarly stipulated. Before evaluation begins, the facility operator defines binding acceptance criteria in the verification plan: a minimum mission completion rate, an upper bound on end-to-end cycle time, and a maximum allowable operator intervention rate, accompanied by sample-size requirements, confidence intervals, and statistical decision rules. A successful mission requires maintaining object identity and physical integrity from retrieval through coworker handover. Cycle time accounting includes transient safety stops, crossing delays, and autonomous replanning; human rescues and aborted deliveries are tracked as explicit mission failures. The safety case stipulates that closed-loop trials of this exact restricted configuration satisfy all three benchmarks. The qualification dossier separates raw neural policy autonomy, system-level task success, and safety interventions into independent metrics, the separation @sec-evaluation-what-measured drew between the policy's own completions and the completions that protection made possible. Minimal-intervention safety filtering may run during nominal task execution; its clamps are counted separately, so they neither mask the policy's shortcomings nor count as safety violations.

With these stipulated evidence packets in hand, the adjudicator can sign a verdict of `COND` (conditional release) for *restricted inspected-route mug delivery*. The physical records support claims C1 through C6 solely within the restricted operating envelope, while the task evaluation shows acceptable operational utility under identical constraints. The adjudicator binds both the physical safety dossier and the capability evaluation to the release manifest, leaving full-speed autonomous transit and remote teleoperation unauthorized. The result is a conditional safety case, not a blanket deployment permit. Invalidating any underlying assumption or breaching a boundary condition immediately returns the verdict to `REFUSE`; conversely, gathering qualified operational telemetry and physical measurements over time can justify expanding the envelope toward full-scale release.

::: {#chk-release-refusal-and-path-to-cond .callout-checkpoint title="Refusal and the path to conditional release"}

Before approving a conditional release of the machine, verify your understanding of how a premise, rather than a calculation, decides a claim:

- [ ] **Premise vs. arithmetic**: Can you explain why the calculated latch force at physical braking onset is not in doubt while the door branch of C1 is still refused?
- [ ] **Unsupported approach**: Can you use @eq-release-trip-indentation and @eq-release-coupled-indentation to show why the operating envelope admits only the guarded door approach?
- [ ] **Refusal as a deliverable**: Can you name, for one refused claim, the measurement that would lift it and the restriction that would remain after a supporting result?
- [ ] **Measured-deceleration estimate**: Suppose loaded stopping trials put the low tail of the deceleration at `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_trial_str` under the same jerk bound. Can you rerun notebook \ref{nbk-release-aisle-spare} at `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_aisle_str` and decide whether that aisle speed can still be signed once $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ is charged?
:::

## Adversarial Review {#sec-release-adversarial-review}

Confirmation bias steers an engineering team's data collection toward nominal conditions where learned models succeed, leaving edge-case hazards untested until live operation exposes them. Suppose the measurements listed in @tbl-16-cond-measurements arrive and, as in the stipulated branch, appear to support a conditional (`COND`) authorization for the mobile manipulator. Before signing, the safety adjudicator submits the safety case to an independent **adversarial review**\index{Adversarial review!definition} tasked with falsifying its warrants. Rather than ratifying a brief, the reviewer actively searches for unsupported warrants, uncharacterized physical transitions, and environmental edge cases that violate the release contract. If an argument collapses on paper when an adversary probes for physical violations, the machine cannot be expected to withstand the hazards of live service.

The review interrogates every evidentiary node in the argument tree using four structured probes. The first challenges **empirical sufficiency**\index{Empirical sufficiency}: whether the physical trials reached the extremes of the operating envelope. Stopping trials with the loaded base on dry concrete, at a friction coefficient near `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_dry_str`, support the warrant that the base achieves its certified deceleration under ideal conditions. The restricted operational mode, however, admits facility floors that the site's inspection regime certifies only down to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`, such as an aisle polished smooth by traffic. In those zones, the base may run at the restricted velocity `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` ceiling. If the trial set contains no loaded stops on such degraded floors at that speed, the warrant for the restricted mode is unsupported. A coverage audit finds on paper the gap that unvetted service would otherwise find against a warehouse rack. The reviewer also checks whether validation trials covered transient execution states across an A/B partition swap, when a newly flashed software bank takes over from the incumbent one (@sec-release-modular-safety-cases). The same check applies to cold-start sensor characteristics before cameras and inertial measurement units reach thermal equilibrium. It applies as well to the operating boundaries of canary units, the small subset of the fleet that first runs a candidate policy (@sec-release-candidate-staging). Finally, the reviewer asks whether site procedures actually keep fluid films out of the corridor throughout the authorized interval, since listing oil outside the envelope does not exclude it from the floor.

The second probe examines **domain transfer**\index{Domain transfer}, targeting claims where synthetic simulation substitutes for direct physical measurement\index{Simulation-to-reality leap}. A vision-based human detector may achieve high recall across synthetic, ray-traced warehouse environments, yet fail on physical hardware when encountering coworkers partially obscured by stretch-wrapped pallets whose specular reflections blind the camera's auto-exposure algorithm. Benchmark recall on curated offline datasets is an indirect proxy metric\index{Proxy metric fallacy} that scores isolated frames rather than the closed-loop physical causal chain running from visual detection to an arrested base. Likewise, a simulation that omits linkage compliance or fieldbus jitter cannot establish tolerance to those physical mechanisms. The reviewer demands empirical evidence from paired hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) trials on target SoC devices connected to chassis dynamometers[^fn-chassis-dynamometer-rollers] and physical bus emulators under real facility illumination, dust, and reflective geometry.

[^fn-chassis-dynamometer-rollers]: **Chassis Dynamometer**\index{Dynamometer!chassis}: Powered rollers under the drive wheels absorb or supply torque, so the base can run at aisle speed on a bench while its drive and braking torques are measured. The rollers, not the floor, set the traction. Dynamometer stops can therefore qualify drive and brake response but say nothing about the friction premise of C3.

The third probe attacks **structural independence**\index{Structural independence}, asking whether the learned model and safety enforcer share hardware resources whose contention could delay sensor delivery or actuation cutoff. On modern robotics edge platforms where neural inference engines and real-time safety enforcers share a single system-on-chip die, internal crossbar interconnects, shared caches, and DRAM memory controllers, unconstrained direct memory access (DMA) transfers from large model forward passes can saturate memory channels. This memory contention induces tail latency spikes that starve deterministic safety enforcer execution ticks, directly invalidating the `{python} ReleaseClaims.t_age_str` observation-age chain of C4. Stress tests and hardware timing analysis under peak synthetic compute and bus loads must establish the worst-case interference bound; unit tests on an otherwise idle bus provide zero evidence of non-interference. The reviewer also checks whether writing frozen edge telemetry ring buffers to non-volatile storage competes with real-time fieldbus DMA buffers across the internal bus fabric. The reviewer inspects watchdog reset circuits for single points of failure and verifies whether the supercapacitor power hold-up circuit supplies enough energy to flush in-flight telemetry buffers to persistent flash when an emergency stop opens the main DC bus contactors.

The fourth probe identifies **unmonitored state drift**\index{Unmonitored state drift}. Mechanical wear alters gearbox compliance\index{Gearbox compliance}[^fn-strainwave-gear-wear] and disrupts the dynamic relationship between commanded motor torque and physical joint motion. The reviewer therefore demands paired wear-state braking and contact traces before accepting the arm-stop premise of the door branch of C1 (@sec-release-case-worked-full). A static motor-current threshold alone cannot prove that a mechanically worn drive train remains inside certified force and stopping limits. The reviewer also checks whether over-the-air updates preserve the persistent hardware calibration partition intact across schema migrations, or whether an OS reflash can silently reset camera extrinsics and joint zeroes to unverified factory defaults. Finally, the probe checks whether thermal bracket motion stays inside the localization allowance; fresh timestamps and unchanged calibration files on disk cannot establish that physical fact.

[^fn-strainwave-gear-wear]: **Strain-Wave Gear Wear**\index{Strain wave gearing!wear}: The arm's joints use strain-wave reducers (@sec-body-transmission-compliance), and in service their flexspline teeth and wave-generator bearing wear. Wear raises lost motion and torsional hysteresis, which adds phase lag between motor and link, so the arm begins to decelerate later and its first contact peak rises.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-compound-defeater
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DIAGNOSTIC THRESHOLDS IN THE COMPOUND DEFEATER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-adversarial-review (compound-defeater paragraph).
# │ Goal: Hold the per-diagnostic thresholds that each anomaly stays inside.
# │ Show: the lens optical-transmission alarm threshold and the camera-mount
# │       deflection fault limit.
# │ How: chapter-local illustrative thresholds; no registry source exists. A
# │      site would take them from the camera's qualification and the mount's
# │      extrinsic-calibration tolerance analysis.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_percent, check

class ReleaseCompoundDefeater:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD: chapter-local inputs ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    optical_transmission_alarm = 0.85  # category: illustrative (lens transmission below which the check alarms; needs source)
    mount_deflection_limit = 0.15 * degree  # category: illustrative (mount deflection fault limit; needs source)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    mount_deflection_limit_deg = mount_deflection_limit.to(degree).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < optical_transmission_alarm < 1, "Transmission threshold is a fraction")
    check(abs(mount_deflection_limit_deg - 0.15) < 1e-12, "Mount deflection limit 0.15 degree")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    transmission_str = fmt_percent(optical_transmission_alarm, precision=0, style="prose")
    mount_limit_str = fmt(mount_deflection_limit_deg, precision=2)
```

Reviewers turn these vulnerabilities into concrete tests by constructing explicit defeaters\index{Defeaters!adversarial review} for each warrant. The hardest failure modes to catch combine minor anomalies that each stay inside their own tolerance bands, the compound faults that @sec-verification-compound-faults derives from shared causes. Consider the mobile manipulator's navigation camera operating with three simultaneous sub-threshold degradations. A light film of dust coats its lens. A mount whose fasteners relaxed within tolerance vibrates as the base crosses floor joints. An interconnect harness flexes at those joints and elevates the bit-error rate across its serializer/deserializer (SerDes) link. Each individual check reads normal. The optical transmission score exceeds its `{python} ReleaseCompoundDefeater.transmission_str` alarm threshold. The mount deflection registers below its `{python} ReleaseCompoundDefeater.mount_limit_str`-degree hardware fault limit. SerDes cyclic redundancy check error counters\index{SerDes!link errors} remain below their warning tripwire. Their timing effects remain contained only if the independent permission path strictly enforces the event-specific observation-age and clock-uncertainty checks of @sec-perception-observation-contract and retains its validated response time. Any hardware or bus interference that defeats that deterministic path is a safety violation under C5, not a benign availability-only event.

The same anomalies compound within spatial estimation. Dimmed contrast reduces tracked visual features, mount vibration adds motion blur and persistent pose bias, and frame drops extend intervals of uncorrected dead reckoning. A systematic pose bias can quietly erode the localization allowance without forcing estimated filter covariances or innovation residuals to breach trip thresholds. The release reviewer therefore challenges the combined error against the qualified uncertainty bound, rather than inferring containment from individually passing scalar diagnostics. A breach of the combined bound consumes part of the stopping reserve and invalidates the release warrant; exhausting the entire stopping margin requires a quantified combined-error scenario. Statistical residual monitoring protects against only the specific faults its qualification shows it can detect, leaving site operational restrictions or independent physical checks to cover the remaining biases.

The review also audits the execution integrity of the permission path, checking whether inference loops or background services can bypass, corrupt, or starve the enforcer or human overrides, the latter covered by claim C6 of @tbl-16-cae-scorecard. Below the proposal boundary, both safety monitors and manual overrides maintain non-preemptible execution priority over learned models. The reviewer asks concrete systems questions: whether a runaway policy thread can exhaust shared memory channels, whether an accelerator-runtime exception can lock a kernel spinlock, and whether a telemetry logging burst can brown out a regulated power rail. The reviewer accepts **permission path**\index{Permission path} independence, and the held-up power rail that carries it on the mobile manipulator, only after reviewing physical fault-injection trials. These trials must show survival under bus saturation, active feed removal, and an abruptly killed proposer task (fault F1), and they must appear in the signed fault records, because C2 claims only the faults the permission path demonstrably survives. A user-space implementation without qualified scheduling, resource isolation, and response mechanisms cannot supply the justified execution bound and fault isolation the reviewer requires.

When an adversarial probe succeeds, the case cannot be salvaged by editing claim descriptions or inserting arbitrary safety margins. The broken warrant is traced to its root systems failure (an uncharacterized physical boundary, an inadequate dataset, or an unmodeled bus latency), and the defect returns to the owning engineering subsystem. For example, a motor-current observer that fails under gearbox compliance returns to the mechanical specification as wear limits and runtime compliance estimation, while bus contention that delays the enforcer returns to the compute architecture as memory partitioning and real-time scheduling. The case returns to the engineering team with its broken warrants named, and only updated boundaries, re-derived stopping distances, and renewed verification reopen formal adjudication.

Adversarial review must also recur periodically, because a case accepted once can erode in service without any single discrete event forcing a new audit. The *normalization of deviance*\index{Normalization of deviance} names that operational erosion, in which anomalies that cause no immediate harm come to be treated as acceptable operating noise rather than as evidence against a warrant [@leveson2011engineering; @vaughan1996challenger] (war story \ref{ws-release-challenger-experience-base-as-boundary}).[^fn-deviance-normalization-origin] On the mobile manipulator, this erosion unfolds silently across months of fleet operation. Localization residuals creep toward the edge of their tolerance. Observation-age watchdog trips are dismissed as nuisance stops. Stopping distances end slightly longer than the initial trials did. Enforcer trips are cleared on the floor without a trace review. When thresholds are widened, margins trimmed for throughput, and alarms suppressed because nothing has yet gone wrong, the gap between the signed envelope and the machine's actual physical behavior widens until a routine disturbance exhausts what remains. The defense is to fix each watched quantity's threshold and response before service begins, as the safety performance indicators of @sec-release-data-curation-flywheel do, so that a run of harmless readings cannot move it.

[^fn-deviance-normalization-origin]: **Normalization of Deviance**\index{Normalization of deviance!origin}: The sociologist Diane Vaughan coined the term in her study of the Challenger launch decision [@vaughan1996challenger]. It names a process rather than a decision, in which each anomaly that caused no harm widened what the next review accepted as normal.

::: {#ws-release-challenger-experience-base-as-boundary .callout-war-story title="Challenger and experience limits (1986)"}
**Context**: The Space Shuttle's solid rocket motors were assembled from cylindrical steel segments whose field joints were sealed by primary and secondary O-rings [@rogers1986challenger]. No learned model appears in this chain. The adjudication failure it records is the exact failure this chapter's verdicts exist to prevent: a launch approved for conditions that the evidence did not cover.

**Mechanism**: The ambient temperature at launch was $36^\circ\text{F}$, 15 degrees colder than any previous launch. O-ring resiliency falls with temperature, and a cold ring returns to shape too slowly to follow the joint gap as ignition pressure opens it. On the eve of launch, engineers at Morton Thiokol, the motor's contractor, recommended against launching below $53^\circ\text{F}$, the O-ring temperature of the coldest previous flight, whose joints had shown the worst blow-by to date. That limit was the outer edge of flight experience, not a qualified bound. NASA managers countered with a qualification temperature that applied to the propellant's bulk temperature rather than to the joint seals.

**Impact**: A combustion gas leak through the right booster's aft field joint, beginning at or shortly after ignition, weakened or penetrated the External Tank. The vehicle broke up about 73 seconds after launch, and all seven crew members died.

**Response**: The presidential Commission attributed the failure to "a faulty design unacceptably sensitive to a number of factors," and temperature heads its list of those factors. It recommended that the joint be changed and that the new design be certified by tests "over the full range of operating conditions, including temperature."

**Systems lesson**: Thiokol management reversed its engineers' recommendation at the urging of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center. Thiokol's vice president of engineering testified, "We had to prove to them that we weren't ready." The burden of proof had inverted: rather than requiring proof that the joint was safe inside its evidence, adjudicators demanded proof that it was unsafe outside the evidence, where no data existed. The Commission also found that O-ring erosion had recurred on earlier flights and that NASA and Thiokol "accepted escalating risk apparently because they 'got away with it last time'" [@rogers1986challenger], so the flight record itself had been read as evidence of safety. A release verdict keeps the burden where the envelope trichotomy puts it. A condition outside the evidence, such as a seal temperature below all flight experience, is unknown, and the verdict refuses it.
:::

The Tempe collision analyzed in @sec-boundary-when-fails rested on an unmeasured premise of the same kind as Challenger's seal temperature. Its vehicle operator was the countermeasure the whole system leaned on, so the premise was that the operator was watching, and nothing measured whether that held. A release case that relies on such a premise must bind its operational response, whether an outright refusal or a restricted case, to verified physical limits, as claim C6 does for authority transfer. Even a case that survives this adversarial review has had its warrants tested only in principle while its verdict still lives on paper. The release manifest turns the surviving argument and the verdict it supports into a signed, tamper-evident record that the machine itself checks before it moves.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The operator-monitoring failures that a human-takeover premise invites, from mode confusion to authority ambiguity, are established in @sec-intervention-failure-modes.
:::

## The Release Manifest {#sec-release-manifest}

A safety case that lives only in static documents or procedural sign-off sheets cannot stop a robot from booting with an unverified policy checkpoint or stale sensor calibrations. To make the verdict enforceable on hardware, the adjudicator's decision is recorded in the **release manifest**\index{Release manifest!definition}\index{Release contract!release manifest}, the fourteenth record in the book's record chain. This signed, tamper-evident data structure binds every upstream engineering contract, the Goal Structuring Notation argument graph, the operating envelope limits, and live standing conditions to the adjudicator's verdict by cryptographic digest. The target platform refuses physical motion whenever runtime binary images, silicon attestation measurements, or underlying qualification data diverge from these signed digests.[^fn-hw-crypto-manifest]

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The residual-claims register, the record that follows the release manifest and ties each premise it leaves open to an operational restriction, is developed in @sec-frontier-residual-claims-register.
:::

The release manifest gathers the engineering contracts established throughout this book. Each upstream record defines an operating boundary or contributes empirical data that the safety case must check; a signature on an isolated contract does not validate the system as a whole. Instead, the manifest links reviewed snapshots of these records into a single argument graph:

1. **Physical plant and timing base:** The limit record (@sec-body-limit-record-schema) documents torque, velocity, and thermal dissipation bounds alongside their qualification data. The proposer's payload requirements (@sec-brain-proposer-information) specify candidate action horizons that feed the handoff record rather than standing as an isolated contract. The handoff record (@sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix) establishes deterministic fieldbus jitter, cycle deadlines, and real-time communication premises.
2. **Data, policy, and behavioral bounds:** The provenance record (@sec-data-schema) captures dataset calibrations, sensor configurations, and operating-domain coverage. The policy manifest (@sec-training-policy-manifest) binds frozen neural network weights to the empirical behavioral bounds proven for that candidate model. The evaluation record (@sec-evaluation-logs) details closed-loop task success rates, human intervention tallies, and stress-tested operational conditions.
3. **Perception, belief, and planning:** The observation contract (@sec-perception-observation-contract) enforces observation freshness and multi-sensor synchronization windows. The belief record (@sec-memory-handoff) specifies geometric state estimates, state covariance, and validity domains. The intent lease (@sec-intent-handoff) records task objectives, spatial tolerances, and preemption conditions. The trajectory record (@sec-planning-trajectory-contract) encodes motion profiles, kinematic seam continuity, execution deadlines, and safe stopping continuations.
4. **Deterministic containment, execution, and verification:** The enforcement record (@sec-enforcement-admitted-command-schema) logs the command stream admitted by runtime safety filters, cleanly separated from the signed enforcement contract that specifies barrier functions and fallback triggers. The placement record (@sec-placement-hardware-allocation) documents the qualified compute scheduling, memory isolation, and processor affinity. The authority record (@sec-intervention-authority-log) documents arbitration switches and fallback outcomes. The fault records (@sec-verification-fault-manifest) index tested fault-injection scenarios alongside known coverage gaps.

Beyond linking these upstream contracts, the release manifest adds its own fields. It carries the root claim, the cryptographic digest of the Goal Structuring Notation argument graph, and binary hashes across all deployed software (spanning learned policy weights, the deterministic enforcer logic in both nominal and restricted modes, and the real-time operating system kernel). It also carries sensor calibration tables, the adjudicator's digital signature, mandatory standing operational conditions, an accumulated lifecycle wear budget of operating hours and load cycles, and a calendar expiration timestamp. All evidence links must resolve to these exact reviewed record digests, organized hierarchically beneath a single evidence root structured as a Merkle hash tree [@merkle1988digital]. Each parent digest is computed from its children's digests, so changing an evidence leaf changes the root that the manifest signs. Only when the hardware root of trust authenticates this complete cryptographic tree will it permit the motor power stages to energize. While traditional release notes or post hoc compliance certificates summarize safety after the fact, the release manifest is an active, machine-checked gate. The robot checks it before closed-loop control begins, and its runtime monitors revoke motor tracking within a bounded detection-and-response window if any underlying evidence or environmental condition expires.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** The release manifest's fields, types, and digests are given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-release.
:::

[^fn-hw-crypto-manifest]: **Cryptographic Manifest and Silicon Attestation**\index{Cryptographic manifest!hardware Root of Trust}: One-time programmable electronic fuses (OTP/eFuse) store the adjudicator's public verification key in silicon, preventing unauthorized software updates from replacing the root of trust. Secure bootstrap validates each early boot stage before handing over execution control [@arbaugh1997secure], while measured boot extends cryptographic measurements into Trusted Platform Module Platform Configuration Registers (TPM PCRs). The hardware verifier checks these measurements against the digests specified in the signed manifest; any unsigned or modified binary image fails attestation and never receives an operational permit.

@Fig-16-release-record routes every release attempt through authentication and physical standing checks before an operating permit can issue. The release gate authenticates the manifest, binary images, and complete set of fault records before verifying current sensor calibration, mechanical maintenance thresholds, and operational design domain conditions. Only an exact cryptographic and physical match enables the plant's certified startup sequence. @Tbl-16-release-authorization lists the gate result for each combination of signed case and standing check, including the single path by which stale calibration still reaches `COND`. A separately signed `COND` case can tolerate a named stale calibration only when its restricted envelope either locks out the motions that depend on that sensor, such as prohibiting base transit when the tote-rack scale is stale, or widens the uncertainty allowance and derates speed to cover worst-case calibration drift. During active motion, any breached condition commands an assessed safe fallback before any switch of software partition (the A/B banks of @sec-release-modular-safety-cases) or electrical isolation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Protocol:** The gate's step-by-step authorization protocol is given in @sec-appendix-systems-release-protocol.
:::

::: {#fig-16-release-record fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Fail-closed release pipeline**: The signed verdict and evidence root pass key, image, and complete fault-record authentication, then current calibration, brake, and operating-envelope checks. Every failure path ends in REFUSE. A valid case reaches UNCOND or COND according to what was signed, and stale calibration reaches COND only through a separately signed restricted case; either way, each proposed action is still checked by the permission path. Attribution: Textbook production team (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)." fig-alt="Left-to-right release path: signed release case, authentication of key chain, images, and fault records, then a check of physical standing. Failed authentication, a false or unknown premise, or stale calibration without a separately signed COND case lead down to a REFUSE bar with permit off and an assessed stop or hold. All valid and current checks lead to a COND box for a signed restricted envelope or an UNCOND box for the full envelope; stale calibration covered by a separately signed COND case also leads to the COND box."}
![](images/svg/fig16_release_record.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Left-to-right release path: signed release case, authentication of key chain, images, and fault records, then a check of physical standing. Failed authentication, a false or unknown premise, or stale calibration without a separately signed COND case lead down to a REFUSE bar with permit off and an assessed stop or hold. All valid and current checks lead to a COND box for a signed restricted envelope or an UNCOND box for the full envelope; stale calibration covered by a separately signed COND case also leads to the COND box."}
:::

\Needspace{22\baselineskip}

| Signed case              | Evidence and standing checks                                                              | Restricted case covering stale calibration | Gate result                                       |
|:-------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| `UNCOND`                 | All valid and current                                                                     | Not needed                                 | Full *proposal* envelope under enforcer; `UNCOND` |
| `COND`                   | All restricted evidence valid and current                                                 | Included if calibration stale              | Signed restricted envelope under enforcer; `COND` |
| `UNCOND` or `COND`       | Fault-record root/signature mismatch, expiry, image mismatch, or unknown physical premise | Any                                        | Permit off; `REFUSE`                              |
| `UNCOND`                 | Calibration stale                                                                         | No                                         | Permit off; `REFUSE`                              |
| Separately signed `COND` | Only the named calibration is stale; restricted evidence and limits valid                 | Yes                                        | Restricted envelope; `COND`                       |
| `REFUSE`                 | Any                                                                                       | Any                                        | Permit off; `REFUSE`                              |

: **Release authorization truth table**: A restricted mode is a distinct authenticated claim, never an unsigned downgrade of the full case. {#tbl-16-release-authorization}

Each empirical evidence leaf in the assurance Merkle tree must identify its raw sensor trace, instrumentation hardware, calibration log, machine configuration, and automated test harness script. Analytical leaves retain their derivations and assumptions; procedural leaves retain the accountable procedure and its validation for the signed envelope. Measured latency profiles enter the safety case as empirical percentiles, whereas deterministic real-time execution guarantees demand the analytically justified upper bounds specified in @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses. Similarly, collaborative object-handover criteria require load-cell time series recorded against standardized anthropomorphic surrogates across specified contact geometries. By cryptographically anchoring these primary records, an independent auditor or verification engine can reproduce the experimental test suite and pinpoint the exact operating boundaries where each safety claim ceases to hold.

The release manifest bounds the physical envelope and hardware configuration under which its verdict remains valid. Modifying a neural policy checkpoint, altering a real-time thread priority, updating a device driver, or replacing an actuator with an unverified component revision immediately invalidates the manifest, requiring a re-adjudicated safety case. On the warehouse mobile manipulator, for example, the manifest enforces signed wear thresholds on harmonic-drive backlash and electromagnetic brake lining thickness derived from stopping-distance and payload trials. Operating envelope tripwires trigger immediate refusal: on-board load cells detect tote-rack overloading beyond rated payload capacity, while facility procedures prevent operation on unmapped or unsurveyed floor surfaces (@tbl-16-odd-invariants). The manifest also encodes the isolated, energy-buffered power rail of the permission path as a standing invariant, running a diagnostic self-test on the hold-up capacitor bank before granting boot authorization. Whenever a runtime sensor detects that a state variable has breached a signed threshold, the hardware permission path interrupts closed-loop trajectory tracking within its certified detection-and-response deadline and brings the system to an assessed fallback state.

To preserve traceability across time, the manifest binds all operational telemetry directly to the exact hardware-software revision that generated it. High-resolution local ring buffers capture boundary excursions for post-incident diagnostics, whereas fleet-wide telemetry summaries reveal systematic mechanical drift across hundreds of operating hours. The curation pipelines examined in @sec-release-data-curation-flywheel must preserve this cryptographic lineage whenever field data is promoted to support a later release case.

During daily operation, edge telemetry logs motor torque residuals, control-loop cycle times, and safety enforcer interventions for trend analysis, while the hardware permission path checks physical invariants on every `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_tick_str` permission tick. If a routine maintenance check measures a stopping distance exceeding the signed clearance budget, or if a camera calibration certificate expires, the release verdict is revoked automatically. Re-flashing an older firmware image cannot compensate for worn mechanical friction pads. Unless an engineer deploys a separately signed restricted case (`COND`) that explicitly accommodates that degraded physical state, the controller executes an assessed emergency stop and locks out autonomous motion until certified maintenance and re-adjudication take place (@tbl-16-release-authorization).

Once its powered stop has brought the base to rest, the warehouse mobile manipulator can reach a quiescent state only after the arm and payload are supported and the assessed holding brakes are engaged before drive power is removed. The base rests stably on the floor, but that support alone does not secure its gravity-loaded arm. For other morphologies, severing motor power is itself the hazard, because the machine collapses under gravity once torque is removed (perspective \ref{capstone-release-humanoid-crucible}).

::: {#capstone-release-humanoid-crucible .callout-perspective title="When removing torque causes the harm"}
**Question**: Which verdict applies when removing torque causes the harm?

A supported wheeled base at rest eliminates its translational kinetic hazard, though its arm and payload still require qualified support. In contrast, an upright bipedal humanoid retains substantial gravitational potential energy. While resting in a support gantry before standing up, a `REFUSE` verdict safely holds the robot in its mechanically supported state. Once balanced upright, however, revoking locomotion authority cannot simply de-energize the actuators without inducing an immediate dynamic fall; safe shutdown requires an active, validated arrest or controlled descent strategy.

* **Torque removal can cause a fall.** An unsupported biped with backdrivable transmissions will collapse if motor currents drop to zero: torque removal leaves gravity-loaded joints without support (@sec-nervous-actuation-authority), and an upright biped without active balance diverges like an inverted pendulum (@sec-nervous-coupled-budget). Consequently, such physical plants cannot treat torque removal as a fail-safe stopping condition unless accompanied by certified passive catches, lock-up brakes, or an external tether.
* **The fall-arrest response is itself an actuation.** Executing a controlled squat, brace, or step-down to bring the robot to rest is itself an active trajectory that requires validated sensorimotor claims, verified timing margins, and fault-tolerance guarantees. In this regime, executing a safe `REFUSE` action depends on the very control systems maintaining upright stability.
* **Wear revokes the running permit.** Degradation in foot-sole rubber traction or increased backlash in planetary gearheads alters the dynamic margin required for emergency balancing. When telemetry signals that physical wear has crossed the threshold certified in the safety case, the runtime supervisor must revoke high-speed dynamic locomotion well before the safety-critical arrest maneuvers degrade below their qualifying safety margins.
:::

::: {#chk-release-student-verdict .callout-checkpoint title="Deriving a verdict from your own measurements"}

@Tbl-16-cond-measurements lists the measurements needed to support a release case but supplies no raw trial results. Make a copy with columns for value, source, provenance, and premise status, fill those columns with empirical data from hardware trials on your own robotic platform or an illustrative benchmark scenario, and evaluate the resulting release verdict:

- [ ] **Provenance and premise status**: For each row, record measured, derived, datasheet, or illustrative provenance; label selected operating requirements as chosen. A derived result retains its inputs and assumptions and remains illustrative when those inputs are illustrative. A selected substitute for an unmeasured brake value is illustrative, whereas a chosen speed cap needs qualified evidence that it fits. A manufacturer's rating is datasheet evidence, not a measurement of this unit. Separately apply the Reader Guide's five premise statuses: established by measurement or derivation, assumed, decided by accountable judgment, unsupported, or outside the threat model. Explain why each credited assumption or restriction is warranted for the signed envelope; a status label grants no authority. Runtime known-true, known-false, and unknown describe current envelope membership, not provenance.
- [ ] **Verdict derivation**: A `COND` case requires adequate support for every relied-on premise: qualified measurements, justified analysis, or validated operating restrictions. Illustrative values alone still support only an actual `REFUSE`. Recompute the base's budget and spare margin from your values. If every relied-on premise has adequate support, name the envelope the `COND` case signs and the premise that keeps the normal mode unsigned. If a relied-on premise lacks adequate support, derive the verdict the table *would* support given the missing evidence, and label that verdict hypothetical.
- [ ] **Artifact label**: Mark the filled table as your own work, whose values license no physical machine.
:::

A release manifest binds the verdict to an explicit, reviewed system configuration. Any later modification, whether retraining a perception head, tightening an actuator torque limit, or swapping a camera lens, breaks that closure and reopens some of the underlying claims. The question the rest of the chapter answers is which ones, and how the machine stays contained while the reopened claims are requalified.

## Maintaining Release Through Updates {#sec-release-deployment-lifecycle}

Continuing the stipulated warehouse branch, suppose the mobile manipulator's restricted mug-delivery policy is retrained to reduce hesitation at the controlled pick station. Pushing that updated checkpoint directly to the fleet would invalidate the signed manifest and expose the machine to unverified bus loads and contact trajectories. Before the candidate neural policy can issue commands to physical actuators, it must pass back through the release decision. A signed safety case establishes which historical evidence remains valid, which hardware-in-the-loop tests must run again, and how the machine maintains physical containment throughout the update.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Every updated checkpoint is a new policy whose earlier evaluations no longer apply, the rule established in @sec-training-real-machine-tuning that gives each one its own manifest and regression evidence.
:::

### Modular safety cases and over-the-air updates {#sec-release-modular-safety-cases}

Retraining a policy directly alters capability evidence, and neural modifications often introduce side effects across the shared hardware platform: increased neural accelerator memory bus traffic, altered sensor frame processing latency, or modified contact force trajectories. An engineer must trace these cross-subsystem dependencies before deciding which containment records remain valid. While **over-the-air (OTA) updates**\index{Over-the-air update!safety case decomposition}\index{Modular safety case!continuous deployment} swap out a named software payload, **modular safety cases**\index{Safety case!modular GSN decomposition} isolate dependencies by recording how each claim relies on specific evidence items and platform assumptions [@denney2015dynamic]. Whenever an update alters an underlying dependency, the modular case shows exactly which safety claims are reopened.

The containment argument is the defense against physical harm. It binds together the plant model, physical sensor limits, worst-case execution budgets, and the independent permission path. Key engineering premises include the bounded tracking error tube $\TrackingErrorBound$, the emergency stopping budget, the passivity barrier for physical contact, and hardware watchdog timing margins. Historical verification records for these containment claims remain valid only if the proposed update preserves the exact operating conditions under which they were measured. For example, replacing a backbone network with a higher-capacity model can increase memory bus contention or cause voltage droop on the power rail even if the deterministic safety-filter binary remains byte-for-byte identical. An unchanged enforcer binary does not imply an unchanged containment argument; its guarantees remain bounded by the validated dynamic envelope $\ForwardInvariantSafeSet$ and the system-level timing margins established during qualification.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The tracking-error tube $\TrackingErrorBound$ that the containment argument consumes as an invariant is established in @sec-enforcement-handoff.
:::

In parallel, the capability argument shows that the robot reliably fulfills its mission within its certified operational design domain. Candidate benchmarking, passive shadow traces, and geofenced closed-loop trials test whether a retrained policy reduces hesitation or improves task throughput. While the low-level enforcer can continuously clamp or reject invalid control proposals to maintain safety, an enforcer that constantly intervenes degrades the robot into an unusable, halting machine. Release engineering therefore evaluates capability and containment together. An update qualifies for fleet dispatch only when the candidate configuration delivers acceptable task performance without undermining the empirical premises supporting its containment envelope.

Modern physical AI platforms preserve configuration integrity during deployment through **dual A/B OS partitioning**\index{Dual A/B OS partitioning!OTA architecture}\index{Atomic update!operating system}. The update agent streams the candidate image onto the inactive storage bank (Bank B) while the incumbent controller continues executing from the active bank (Bank A). Activating the newly flashed partition requires an assessed stationary update state. The robot must be parked with its payload supported. Battery reserves must exceed with margin the energy needed for re-flashing and post-boot self-tests. The independent safety supervisor must hold all motor drives unpowered or mechanically locked so the robot cannot move during bootloader cutover. Hardware watchdogs govern the runtime decision to commit or abort this cutover (@sec-release-verdicts-ota-watchdogs). A single fleetwide signing key is a single point of compromise, because an attacker who extracts that key from one compromised endpoint could sign arbitrary firmware for every robot in the field. Update architectures therefore use role-separated signing structures where distinct root, targets, and release keys live on separate, hardware-isolated machines. The Update Framework (TUF) pioneered this design, and Uptane extended it to automotive and robotics systems where heterogeneous electronic control units require independently authenticated firmware images [@samuel2010survivable; @kuppusamy2016uptane].

Overwriting firmware must never destroy the physical calibration history of an individual robot. **Persistent hardware calibration parameter retention**\index{Hardware calibration!persistent parameter retention}\index{Parameter partition!decoupled storage} separates machine-specific measurements from generic operating system binaries, preventing a **calibration clashing failure**\index{Calibration clashing failure}. Camera intrinsic matrices ($\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix$), extrinsic sensor transformations ($[\DirectionalCosineMatrix \mid \RigidTransformTranslation]$), kinematic joint zero-point offsets, and motor torque constants ($\MotorTorqueConstant$) reflect the mechanical and electrical geometry of an individual machine and drift over time with vibration, thermal cycling, and wear. Storing these values in a dedicated, wear-leveled, non-volatile parameter partition keeps calibration intact when an OS image is flashed. When a firmware update introduces a revised parameter schema, the migration utility writes the transformed schema into a new record while preserving the legacy block, allowing direct rollback to the prior image-parameter pair. Cryptographic checksums verify the bit-level integrity of these stored calibration blocks, while physical self-tests at field release verify that the stored parameters still match the physical machine.

Finally, **forensic traceability**\index{Forensic traceability!release provenance}\index{Release manifest!cryptographic provenance} links every running OS image, policy checkpoint, and calibration partition to its training provenance, compiler flags, and reviewed HIL regression records through the signed release manifest (@sec-release-manifest). When an unexpected field intervention or trajectory excursion occurs, these links let incident investigators reconstruct the exact configuration running at that millisecond and determine which safety warrants need re-examination. While a cryptographic digest confirms identity, isolating the physical root cause requires detailed sensor traces and causal analysis.

### Staging candidate policies before release {#sec-release-candidate-staging}

Software simulation models timing and electrical behavior only to the accuracy of its mathematical approximations; it cannot catch memory-bus contention, fieldbus noise, or inverter thermal sag on the real processor and drive electronics. A candidate policy must therefore repeat the **hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) regression gates**\index{Hardware-in-the-loop!regression gates}\index{Release engineering!HIL regression testing} affected by its changes on a physical test bench under full thermal and electrical load. The bench tests the specific interference and fault mechanisms on which release claims depend:

1. **Worst-case execution time (WCET) and scheduling jitter**: Profiling whether safety filter evaluations complete within their hard real-time deadlines ($\WorstCasePermissionCycleTime \le \CompletionDeadline$) while neural workloads drive peak memory crossbar contention and DMA transfers, the falsification campaign of @sec-placement-testing-separation.
2. **Deterministic bus arbitration**: Measuring fieldbus communication jitter and cyclic transmission integrity across physical EtherCAT or CAN FD networks under simulated telemetry broadcast floods and electrical noise injection.
3. **Power-stage thermal dynamics and current ripple**: Verifying that high-frequency control chatter or torque ripple proposed by the candidate policy does not induce excessive inverter switching losses, DC rail voltage sag, or thermal runaway in motor windings (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles).
4. **Hardware fault-injection survivability**: Validating that physical line breaks, power supply brownouts, or deserializer frame dropouts deterministically trigger the hardware watchdog and safe-stop sequence within certified timing budgets before motor power stages can be damaged.

A candidate policy advances through bench staging only when every required regression test passes and empirical records confirm that timing and physical margins remain intact. Observing zero deadline overruns during a finite bench campaign does not by itself establish a mathematical upper bound on worst-case execution time, nor does it show how the policy will behave on the warehouse floor. In cloud software engineering, blue-green deployment can reduce downtime by preparing a replacement cluster and redirecting traffic after readiness checks. In physical AI, however, blue-green cutover cannot happen mid-stride or at speed. Swapping active control authority between an incumbent controller and a candidate policy while mass is moving requires managing actuator state continuity, motor winding back-EMF, and dynamic tracking tubes (@sec-intervention-command-steps). De-energizing motor windings or inducing sudden torque steps causes severe mechanical shock loads ($\GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia \LinkAngularAcceleration$) and loss of traction. An unvalidated policy also cannot be granted partial motor authority in a populated warehouse to "canary test" edge-case performance.

Safe predeployment staging instead relies on **shadow mode deployment**\index{Shadow mode deployment!definition}, the shadow-operation evidence regime of @sec-evaluation-four-regimes applied to a release candidate. The incumbent controller $\pi_{\text{incumbent}}$ supplies proposals, while the independent enforcer retains sole actuator-output ownership and checks each command before fieldbus dispatch. Concurrently in the background, the candidate neural policy $\pi_{\text{candidate}}$ executes on the host compute SoC, consuming identical live sensor streams $\MultimodalObservation_{t}$ within its qualified shared-resource budget and computing what control command $\CandidateControlCommand_t \sim \pi_{\text{candidate}}(\MultimodalObservation_{t})$ it would have proposed.
